### Reviewer 1

The authors provide an interesting field and genetic study of the possibility of using M. cheesmanii as a potential wild crop relative to create new banana hybrids that may be resistant to different strains of Fusarium wilt (especially the virulent TR4). The paper also provides a range of background information on the genetics of banana evolution, genetic variation in eBSV and RGA2, and a multi-omics insight into black pseudostem coloration. These three sections are interesting and provide supporting information relevant to the use of M. cheesmanii as a potential WCR source for new hybrids.
I especially commend the authors' intent to use more traditional crop breeding techniques involving WCRs as a means of generating new hybrids/crosses, rather than gene editing.
There are some methodological issues with the paper as written:
1. The first results section provides insights into the susceptibility of crop progenitor species to most modern cultivars - essentially AA, AB, BB, AAB, ABB and AAA - with triploids dominating modern subsistence and cash crop cultivation globally. However, and somewhat oddly given the subsequent direction of the paper, a Cavendish cultivar (AAA) is chosen to demonstrate the susceptibility of cultivars to Foc_TR4. Given that M. cheesmanii is B clade/genome, and given the rest of the paper deals with two new hybrids derived from ABB cultivars, it would make sense to present data here for those hybrids susceptibility to Foc_TR4. Incidentally, it may also be worth discussing the pre-existing contribution of M. cheesmanii to some AAB and ABB hybrids - as I believe there is some.
2. Throughout the paper, M.a ssp. malaccensis is used as the main Musa acuminata exemplar, which is okay - but would Musa acuminata ssp. banksii be more pertinent - as potentially it is the original M. acuminata domesticate that contributes especially to AAA cultivars and others (following a host of CIRAD genetics papers). It would seem that the role of M. a. ssp. mal. is later in the derivation of major cultivar groups - although some of the northerly AA and AAA cultivars, as well as some AAB and ABB have contributions from the westerly M. a ssp. Even though there may be some debate about all this, regarding the relative contributions of different M. a. ssp, the choice of M.a. ssp. mal as the representative of the A genome contribution to modern cultivars should be more clearly explained.
3. lines 193-197 - a range of value judgements are made here regarding the growing and fruiting quality of the new derived hybrids, which are problematic. Why state 'best offspring' - rather just delete the word 'best' and retain the enhanced traits aspect (which you then state). Regarding fruit - and this recurs throughout the paper - you say 'excellent taste' (line 197) without providing any evidence for this. As raised in the paper, one of the major problems with banana breeding programs has been the derivation of new cultivars that are Foc resistant, while also retaining fruit quality. the latter is the hardest aspect to breed for - such that it is commercially viable (ie, as a replacement for the Foc susceptible Cavendish). I think we need more here to establish why the fruit quality is excellent - how measured - what was the control group and so on. Alternatively, maybe leave this as something to be determined through fruit quality tests - but state that the initial results are promising.
4. lines 271-278 - the link of banana evolution to glacial cycles over the last 800,000 years or so is extremely tenuous. Your figure 3c indicates three glacial events for the last <800,000 years, whereas there have been 8-9 glacial cycles in that time - so why these three? Furthermore, the actual logic of the argument is limited - as the effects of glacial cycles are usually felt at higher altitudes and latitudes, rather than in lowland tropical locales (where effects can be somewhat more muted). It may affect mid-altitude species and also those on exposed continental shelfs during lower sea levels, but that is quite an argument to make (and it is not made). So, currently, the invocation of glacial cycles to understand banana demographic history/genetics is selective (why 3 not 7-8 glacial cycles) and requires justification (what is the process?).
5. Generally the figures are of a high quality and informative. My only concerns focus on Figure 3 - which is hard to follow, even with the caption.
- I think the figure needs to be rearranged - as effectively panel d could go at the end of the two panels in b (and why two panels in b) - as the three panels in total (two in b and one in d) actually correspond and flow from one another.
- the different ordering of chromosomes in panel a and d is confusing - and I think the chromosomes in panel d should be labelled to avoid any confusion (as these just increase from 1,2, 3 and so on, whereas those in panel a do not).
- again, panel c - I am not sure that the glacial cyclicity element works here - and if the glacial cycles are taken off - what are you trying to show? Maybe state it more clearly. Also, your caption implies the diagram shows the reduction in effective population size during the last 400-500,000 years in A genome species most markedly. However, why associated with glacial cyclicity - as effective population sizes for most species increase markedly before this reduction - and yet this is still within the period of Pleistocene glacial cyclicity (over 20 within the last 2.6 million years).
These are my substantive comments. I am not a geneticist and so cannot comment on the genetics methods and detail, but I hope my comments are useful for refining the logic of argument to the general readership of this journal.

### Reviewer 2

I read the manuscript titled "Going wild in banana breeding: the cross-compatibility and multi-omics of Musa cheesmanii" with great interest. I should underline that my expertise is mainly in genome assembly rather than banana genomics. I would like to congratulate the authors on this genome assembly. Even though it is of low complexity, they generated a substantial amount of diverse sequencing data and produced a high-quality reference genome for Musa cheesmanii. Here are my main concerns about this study.
Sequencing Data and Assembly Methods:
The authors generated interesting sequencing data and combined two long-read technologies with Hi-C data, which is better than the current standard. However, they used methods that are generally not employed for reference genomes: NextPolish and TGS-GapCloser. Most genomes from projects like VGP, dToL, ATLASea, or BGE are based on purge_dup (instead of Purge_Haplotigs), YaHS (instead of 3D-DNA), and are manually curated using Pretext (instead of Juicebox). This is not a problem at all, but the authors should provide adequate validation of their assembly at different stages.
I would expect a supplementary table containing standard analyses such as BUSCO, Merqury, and KAT for the assembly obtained at each step: raw assembly, polished assembly, purged assembly, gap-closed assembly, and final assembly. This would allow monitoring the impact of each tool on the assembly.
Use of TGS-GapCloser:
The authors used TGS-GapCloser, which is rarely used in the generation of reference genomes. I understand the temptation to get an assembly without gaps, but I would be very cautious about the accuracy of these gap-closed regions. The authors should clearly indicate their position in the genome and provide at least local validation using long-read coverage and Hi-C map visualization.
Chromosomal Inversion:
I was curious to know if the inversion detected in chromosome 5 with Macuminata and Mschizocarpa occurs at the same position in Musa cheesmanii. Can the authors provide more information and details about this inversion? Validation of breakpoints would be of interest.
Data Availability:
The assembly and gene annotation were not available from the NGDC database nor from the Banana Genome Hub. Please provide access to the genome.
Minor Points:
Line 143: Is 34.3 days correct? Should it be less?
Lines 212-214: The analysis of GC content along the chromosomes is not a standard method to assess the quality of an assembly. Please remove this sentence.
Lines 233-240: This paragraph is a bit redundant and can be reduced.
Section on Structural Variations (Lines 279-303): This section is very descriptive and can be reduced without changing the scientific content of the article.
Lines 610-613: Please add more description on the Hi-C library preparation.
Line 640: The telomeric sequence in plants is T3AG3, not T3G3A as mentioned.

### Reviewer 3

Review of Manuscript ID NCOMMS-25-27107-T by Liu and colleagues.
Manuscript title: Going wild in banana breeding: the cross-compatibility and multi-omics of Musa cheesmanii
The manuscript presents a detailed investigation into the crossbreeding potential of Musa cheesmanii, highlighting its resistance to Fusarium wilt TR4 and its value as a male parent in banana improvement. The study also contributes a high-quality telomere-to-telomere genome assembly and complementary multi-omics data, providing useful insights into genome evolution and pigmentation traits in Musa species. The findings will be of interest to those working in banana breeding and genomics. However, the manuscript, in its current form, does not align with the broad conceptual scope and interdisciplinary impact required by Nature Communications. We recommend considering resubmission to a more specialised journal focused on crop improvement, plant genomics, or biotechnology, where the work will be more appropriately positioned.
Please see our comments below for further improvement.
Thank you.
General comments
This study contributes meaningfully to banana breeding research by integrating crossbreeding experiments, high-quality genomic data, and multi-omics analyses. The successful hybridisation of Musa cheesmanii with ABB cultivars highlights its potential to enhance disease resistance and yield. Notably, the authors report the first telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly for this species, which adds a valuable resource to the Musa genomics community.
The comparative genomic analysis provides useful insights into chromosomal rearrangements and structural variation among Musa species. Additionally, the integration of transcriptomic and metabolite profiling to investigate pseudostem pigmentation adds depth to the study. The anthocyanin pathway analysis offers a novel angle, although its biological significance remains unclear and may require further refinement.
The rationale for investigating pseudostem colouration is not convincingly presented, and the relevance of this trait to banana breeding is not well established. A more compelling case could have been made by prioritising traits directly linked to agronomic performance, such as disease resistance. For example, a comparative evolutionary analysis of resistance (R) gene families between M. cheesmanii and other Musa species with available high-quality genomes would have added greater value and relevance.
Overall, the manuscript is well-structured, with a logical flow from the problem statement to actionable conclusions, supported by data across multiple levels of analysis.
The use of the first person “we” should be avoided.
Abstract
The abstract provides a clear overview of the study’s objectives and highlights key outcomes, including Fusarium wilt resistance and the generation of productive hybrids. However, the manuscript lacks quantitative data to support several claims in the abstract, particularly those related to hybrid traits such as extended shelf life. Including specific metrics would enhance the credibility of these statements. Furthermore, phrases such as “breakthrough in genetic diversity” are overstated and not fully justified by the results presented. The expression “fully completed genome” is redundant; more precise terminology such as “gap-free” or “telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly” is recommended.
Introduction
The introduction provides a relevant overview of banana breeding challenges and the limited genetic diversity in modern cultivars. The inclusion of Fusarium wilt is appropriate, although it should be explicitly stated that Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense tropical race 4 (TR4) is currently the most devastating fungal disease affecting global banana production. The challenges associated with the activation of endogenous Banana streak virus (eBSV) sequences in hybrids are briefly mentioned, but their impact is understated. In practice, the risk of eBSV activation severely limits the use of B-genome cultivars in breeding programs, and this critical constraint deserves greater emphasis.
These issues help frame the rationale for exploring wild relatives like Musa cheesmanii as alternative genetic resources. However, the specific knowledge gap addressed by this study is not clearly defined. It remains unclear whether M. cheesmanii has never been previously used in breeding programs, or whether this work represents the first comprehensive analysis of its cross-compatibility and genomic potential.
The claim that this study presents “the first fully completed genome in banana” is unsubstantiated and should be revised. Similar high-contiguity, telomere-to-telomere assemblies have already been published for other Musa species, and this work should be positioned in relation to that context.
Finally, the rationale for focusing exclusively on anthocyanins as the drivers of stem pigmentation is weak. Other phenolic compounds, particularly those that contribute to dark or black coloration through oxidative polymerisation (e.g. catechols, L-DOPA, caffeic acid), should also be considered. A more balanced introduction would acknowledge these alternative pathways and set the stage for a broader investigation of pigmentation mechanisms.
Results
This section presents a substantial amount of data, but its impact is limited by gaps in quantitative reporting, inconsistent methodology, and several unsupported claims. While genome assembly and comparative genomics are handled well, data presentation regarding hybrid performance, pigmentation, and qPCR validation require some revision.
Phenotypic evaluation and hybrid performance
• Table 2 lacks critical information. It does not include plant height data, sample sizes, replication numbers, or any measures of variability such as standard deviations. Additionally, the parental line data are absent, making it difficult to contextualise and interpret the performance of the hybrids.
• The number of plants evaluated for each hybrid and parental line should be explicitly reported in both the table and the main text.
• Terms such as “normal seedling percentage” and “seed generation percentage” (lines 173-175) are vague and require clearer definitions to ensure the data are interpretable to readers unfamiliar with the breeding system described.
• The shelf-life claim on line 197, which states an “extended shelf life of 6-9 days,” is not supported by quantitative data. This claim should be backed with comparative measurements between hybrids and parent lines. Similarly, the reference to “excellent taste” is subjective and should be removed unless supported by a sensory evaluation using an established methodology.
Disease resistance data
• While Table 1 presents disease resistance data clearly for the parental lines, no equivalent data are provided for the hybrids. This omission limits the strength of the claim that resistance traits have been successfully transferred.
• A new table should be added to report disease resistance data for the hybrids using the same scoring or index system used in Table 1.
• The “Disease Index” formula referenced in Table 1 should be added to the “Methods” section at least, to ensure transparency and reproducibility.
• The use of “NS” to denote “no symptoms” is inconsistent across the table as NS also appear in the IP column.
Metabolite analysis and pigmentation
• The authors report the detection of numerous low-abundance anthocyanins (Figure S18). However, the authors have not provided any detail in their methods to evaluate the reliability of their compound identification or quantification. Critical information missing includes sample preparation protocols, chromatographic separation parameters, MS/MS acquisition settings, and criteria used for compound identification. This lack of transparency is particularly concerning given that several anthocyanins share identical m/z values, making chromatographic resolution and MS/MS spectral interpretation essential for accurate compound differentiation. For metabolite quantification the authors should report whether they used any standards for quantification. Without this information, it is difficult to assess whether the low-abundance signals are from true analytes or are analytical artifacts.
• Following this, the authors suggest that the black stem colouration is due to accumulation of specific anthocyanins presented in Supplementary figure 18b. Whilst the authors have reported statistical significance in compound accumulation, given their extremely low abundance (for example 0.02 ug/g pelargonidin-3-O-arabinoside) compared to other identified compounds (eg. in S18a procyanidin B2 is reported at around 300 ug/g for both M. cheesmanii and the green stemmed Musa acuminata) is this difference likely to be biologically relevant in creating the black stem phenotype? The authors should note that dark brown or black colouration can come from sources other than anthocyanins. Oxidation of phenolics which have two neighbouring hydroxyl groups can lead to the formation of quinone-like structure which can further undergo polymerisation making brown/black colouration. Examples include caffeic acid, catechol, catechin, dopamine and L-DOPA. Dopamine and L-DOPA have previously been detected in various banana tissues at high concentrations. Additionally, as the first 3 compounds share many of the genes/enzymes with the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway, the authors should consider adjusting the manuscript (including transcriptome analysis) to encompass all phenolics rather than only anthocyanins.
Transcriptomic validation (qPCR)
• The claim that transcriptomic findings were validated by qPCR (lines 377-378) is misleading. For example, the gene F3’H is not statistically significant based on Supplementary Figure 15a, and there is no presented qPCR data for PAL2 or BGLU26, even though these genes are mentioned.
• The qPCR methodology is also not described. The manuscript should include details about cDNA synthesis protocols, primer sequences, and amplification conditions in the “Methods” section.
• To support transparency and reproducibility, the authors should also consider providing raw Ct values as a supplementary table.
• Supplementary Figure 8a appears to be nearly identical to Figure 4a in the main text. To avoid redundancy, one of these figures should be removed.
Minor revisions and editorial suggestions
• The authors should ensure consistent terminology and formatting across all tables and figures, particularly for labels and abbreviations.
• All abbreviations should be defined upon first use in each table or figure, even if they are explained elsewhere in the manuscript. For example, “eBSV” should be redefined as “endogenous banana streak virus” where it first appears.
Discussion
This is a good discussion supported by a solid foundation of relevant literature.
Certain sections, such as the paragraph beginning at line 509, primarily summarise results rather than examining their broader implications within the context of existing research.
The discussion does not consider some of the practical challenges associated with the use of M. cheesmanii in breeding programs. These may include low hybrid recovery rates, the potential for linkage drag, and the complexity of backcrossing strategies. Additionally, phrases such as “revolutionary breakthrough” and “remarkable productivity” are used in the text without sufficient supporting evidence and do not align with the otherwise analytical tone.
Expanding the discussion to include resistance genes, specifically identifying the types of loci involved, could add value. Comparing these loci to those found in other published Musa genomes, and considering their potential implications for breeding strategies, would provide additional depth and relevance.
The structure of the discussion may be improved by the inclusion of subheadings to support clarity and assist reader navigation. Several paragraphs are lengthy and would benefit from being divided into smaller units. Although the intended audience is likely to have technical expertise, certain terms could be clarified to increase accessibility. For example, “eBSV” could be restated as “endogenous banana streak virus,” and terms such as “segregation distortion” and “structural heterozygosity” could be accompanied by short explanations.
The presentation of data may be strengthened through brief agronomic interpretation. For instance, a girth to height ratio of 0.225 could be described as exceeding the threshold associated with resistance to lodging.
Finally, the discussion could also benefit from consideration of future directions, such as whether similar traits may be found in other underutilised Musa species or what risks could emerge from the widespread deployment of M. cheesmanii in breeding programs.
Methods
Critical methodological details are missing in several areas, which limits the reproducibility and rigour of the study.
The description of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense TR4 inoculation lacks essential information. The origin of the fungal strain, its vegetative compatibility group (VCG), and the inoculation protocol (particularly the spore concentration and method of application) are not provided. In addition, the criteria used to evaluate external and internal symptoms of infection, and how disease severity was scored or calculated, are not adequately described.
Hybrid evaluation is similarly underdeveloped. Terms such as “seed set,” “seed generation,” and “normal seedling” (lines 592-593) are ambiguous and require precise definitions. The section describing hybrid assessment (lines 592-597) lists variables that were evaluated but does not explain how these measurements were conducted. Sample sizes for hybrid offspring are also not reported, and replication details are entirely missing.
The anthocyanin analysis lacks transparency, with key methodological details missing. Specific recommendations for improving this section are outlined in the Results critique above.
qPCR validation of transcriptomic data is not described at all. There is no information about cDNA synthesis, primer sequences, qPCR reaction conditions, or normalisation strategies. To improve transparency and reproducibility, the authors should include these details in the methods and provide raw Ct values in a supplementary table.
Finally, a specific section on statistical analysis should be included.
Tables and figures
• The overall quality and readability of the tables and figures is good. However, Figures 1 and 2 would benefit significantly from higher-resolution images and improved formatting to enhance visual clarity.
• In Figure 2, scale bars are missing from all panels and should be added to ensure interpretability, particularly for morphological comparisons.
• In Table 2, the definition of “plant stature” is placed in the footnotes, should also be added to the main text (Methods). Table 2 needs to include data from parental lines, plant height measurements, standard deviations, and the number of replicates. A new table reporting hybrid disease resistance should be created, modelled on Table 1.
• Figure 4, panel (e), which presents RGA2 polymorphisms, requires clearer labelling to highlight the nonsense mutation (T→A at 3,687 bp).
• Figure 4 and Supplementary Figure 8 present nearly identical phylogenetic trees. To avoid redundancy, one of these should be removed.
• Figure legends throughout should be made more descriptive, especially when referring to multi-panel figures.
End of report

### Reviewer 4

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

## Paper

## Abstract

Bananas (Musa spp.) are crucial for food security, but modern cultivars derived from few wild species and propagated vegetatively possess low genetic diversity, and weak disease resistance. Identifying new parental lines is therefore essential for banana breeding. Here we show that Musa cheesmanii exhibits high resistance to Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense tropical race 4. We cross it with two Musa ABB cultivars popular in China, 'Yulin' and 'Jinyu'. The resulting hybrids exhibit enhanced disease resistance, high yield, desirable pulp taste, and extended shelf-life, underscoring the breeding value of this wild species. Additionally, a telomere-to-telomere, gap-free genome of M. cheesmanii is assembled, with multi-omics analyses offering insights into its diversification, black pseudo-stem coloration, and disease resistance. Overall, M. cheesmanii is a promising male parent for enhancing genetic diversity and improving banana cultivars.

---

## Introduction

Crop wild relatives (CWRs) are crucial for modern breeding programs as they provide essential genetic diversity that cultivated crops often lack1. These wild species carry crucial genes that can help overcome the genetic bottlenecks in cultivated crops, enhancing their resilience to climate change, pests, and diseases while improving yield and quality. Thus, protecting and utilizing the genetic diversity of CWRs is vital for the sustainability and adaptability of global agriculture.

Bananas (Musa spp.) are among the world's most important crops and are critical to food security in tropical and subtropical regions. However, global production is increasingly threatened by Fusarium wilt, a fungal disease caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc), with tropical race 4 (Foc_TR4) currently recognized as the most devastating fungal pathogen affecting banana cultivation worldwide2,3. Bananas' susceptibility to climate change, pest infestations, and diseases like Fusarium wilt highlights the urgent need for cultivar improvement to ensure sustainable production. The Musa genus, with approximately 70 wild species, is classified into two sections: sect. Musa (n=11) and sect. Callimusa (n=7/9/10)4,5. Most of the over 1,000 cultivated banana varieties originated from inter- and intra-specific hybridizations involving Musa acuminata (A genome), Musa balbisiana (B genome), and Musa schizocarpa (S genome)6-10. The majority of edible banana cultivars are found to be triploids (AAA, AAB and ABB), which have been selected by humans for their parthenocarpy11. Therefore, it appears that the genetic constitution of modern banana cultivars is derived from a very limited number of wild banana species with diverse hybridization history6,8,10,12. Most of the observed variation arises from variable mosaic contributions of different M. acuminata subspecies6,12. Additionally, the reliance on vegetative propagation (such as sucker division or tissue culture) in cultivated bananas has further narrowed genetic diversity, consequently weakened their resistance to numerous challenges3.

Hybrid breeding, which involves crossing two genetically distinct parents to combine their desirable traits, is a common approach for enhancing genetic diversity and improving crop characteristics. In the market, hybrid cultivars are generally more widely accepted than genetically modified varieties due to consumer preference for traditional breeding methods, which also serve as the primary approach for banana cultivar improvement. However, banana crossbreeding programs, which began nearly a century ago in Trinidad, continue to face significant challenges, such as the crop's triploid nature (resulting in low fertility) and lengthy breeding cycles. These challenges often result in breeding programs that take up to two decades to develop a locally acceptable cultivar, yet a commercially viable cultivar remains elusive13,14. Banana wild relatives are a promising source of genetic variation, offering a wide gene pool to enhance banana resilience against biotic and abiotic stresses. They typically produce numerous seeds and have large anthers with abundant pollen, making them ideal paternal resources in breeding programs. However, unlike major crops such as rice, wheat, and soybean, wild relatives have been used only to a very limited extent in banana breeding programs1. Traditionally, the diploid ancestors, subspecies of M. acuminata and M. balbisiana, are selected as the male parents.

M. acuminata comprises several subspecies, including banksii, malaccensis, zebrina, and burmannica. Among them, M. acuminata ssp. banksii is the major contributor to all cultivated bananas followed M. acuminata ssp. zebrina. Although M. acuminata ssp. burmannica, particularly the accession 'Calcutta 4', is not commonly found in natural cultivars, it has been widely used in breeding programs due to its strong disease resistance. Interestingly, malaccensis is also known for its high resistance to Foc, as well as a significant contributor to several cultivar groups, including AAA (e.g., Cavendish, Gros Michel, Red), AAB (e.g., Pome, Silk), and ABB (e.g., Pisang Awak)12. The use of M. balbisiana is severely constrained by the risk of activating endogenous banana streak virus (eBSV), especially under stress or during in vitro culture, which can lead to spontaneous viral expression in hybrids and compromise plant health and yield15-17. This genetic instability not only limits the use of B-genome cultivars in banana improvement programs but also hampers global germplasm exchanges due to the risk of eBSV activation into an infectious episomal form. Therefore, identifying potential male parents from banana wild relatives is promising for developing superior cultivars, given their significant role in enhancing cultivar diversity and their limited use in current breeding programs.

Species closely related to M. balbisiana (hereafter referred to as B-lineage species) have demonstrated high levels of resistance to Foc_TR418,19. Among the B-lineage species, Musa cheesmanii is phylogenetically close to M. balbisiana18. While it shares many morphological traits with M. balbisiana, M. cheesmanii can be distinguished by its significantly larger seeds, which are nearly twice the size, along with its more open bunch structure and upward-pointing fruits20. M. cheesmanii is a wild banana species native to Medog, China, the low-altitude southern slopes of the Himalayas, and the neighboring northeastern region of India20. It thrives in subtropical and tropical mountain forests, where it experiences cooler temperatures, higher humidity, and variable light levels compared to lowland species. This species features a tall (4 to 8 meters in height) and black pseudo-stem. The black appearance of the pseudo-stem is likely attributed to the accumulation of anthocyanins and/or the oxidative polymerization of phenolic compounds (e.g., catechols, L-DOPA, caffeic acid)21-23. According to our field observation, M. cheesmanii exhibits strong resistance to Fusarium wilt, as it remains disease-free when grown in soil contaminated with Foc_TR4; moreover. In addition, M. cheesmanii is highly productive, with its bunch weight exceeding that of most wild bananas by more than three-fold. Therefore, M. cheesmanii emerges as a highly promising candidate for use as a male parent in future banana breeding programs. Its use could significantly broaden the genetic base of bananas, leading to the development of high-yield, disease-resistant varieties. However, M. cheesmanii has not been systematically examined in banana breeding research, and its cross-compatibility and genetic characteristics remain unexplored, indicating the need for in-depth characterization to support its use in breeding.

In this study, offspring are generated by crossbreeding M. cheesmanii with two Musa ABB cultivars, 'Yulin' and 'Jinyu'. Cross-compatibility is assessed between three wild banana species, including M. acuminata, M. balbisiana, and M. cheesmanii, and the two ABB cultivars. Specifically, the ability of the wild species to serve as male parents in the crossbreeding process is evaluated. The results indicate that M. cheesmanii represents a promising male parent for banana breeding, as its hybrid offspring with ABB cultivars demonstrate enhanced Foc_TR4 resistance, high yield, favorable pulp taste, and extended shelf-life. A telomere-to-telomere (T2T) gap-free genome assembly of M. cheesmanii is also presented. Following this, we perform a multi-omics analysis to deepen genomic insights into the evolution of bananas, the molecular mechanisms underlying black pseudo-stem coloration, and the species' potential genetic variations related to disease resistance. Overall, M. cheesmanii is identified as a promising male parent for banana hybrid breeding, marking an advancement in the highly challenging field of banana breeding. Additionally, the comprehensive genome features of M. cheesmanii provide a foundation for future banana breeding efforts, paving the way for improved cultivars with enhanced traits.

---

## Results

Response of M. cheesmanii and its offspring to Foc_TR4 infection
Fusarium wilt resistance was evaluated under both greenhouse and field conditions using Foc_TR4. The tested accessions included three wild bananas (M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis, M. balbisiana, and M. cheesmanii), two banana cultivars belonging to the ABB genome group ('Jinyu', Pisang Awak group, and 'Yulin', Dajiao group), their respective hybrids with M. cheesmanii ('Haifen No. 1' and 'Haijiao No. 1'), and a susceptible control, the Cavendish cultivar 'Baxijiao' (Table 1, Fig. 1). Several parameters were measured to evaluate Fusarium wilt resistance, including the incubation period (IP), which represents the average time from inoculation to symptom onset in greenhouse tests. Additionally, disease incidence was monitored by calculating the proportion of plants exhibiting external and internal Fusarium wilt symptoms out of the total number of plants evaluated. Disease severity and the disease index (DI) were also evaluated based on external symptoms and rhizome discoloration.

The IP of each accession under greenhouse conditions was shown in Table 1. The IP for the susceptible control 'Baxijiao' was the shortest among all the accessions tested, with symptoms appearing after an average of 34.3 days after inoculation (dai). M. balbisiana and M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis also exhibited Fusarium wilt symptoms, but their IPs were 3.5 and 10.8 days longer than that of 'Baxijiao', respectively. In contrast, M. cheesmanii showed no external symptoms, preventing us from calculating its IP. The IP of 'Jinyu' was 34.5 dai, comparable to that of 'Baxijiao', whereas its hybrid offspring 'Haifen No. 1' exhibited a longer IP of 38.3 dai. Similarly, 'Yulin' show a relatively long IP of 45.5 dai, while its hybrid 'Haijiao No. 1' displayed no external symptoms during the tested period. As expected, the 'Baxijiao' and 'Jinyu' showed the most severe symptoms of Fusarium wilt (Table 1, Fig. 1a, e), confirming their high susceptibility to Foc_TR4. The disease severity in the three wild relatives and the other cultivars was lower than in 'Baxijiao', yet Foc_TR4 still colonized these plants, causing characteristic Fusarium wilt symptoms, especially in M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis, M. balbisiana, and the hybrid 'Haifen No. 1' (Fig. 1b, c, f). Using the four-class rating scale developed in our previous study19, M. cheesmanii and the hybrid offspring 'Haijiao No. 1' were categorized as highly resistant, as no Fusarium wilt symptoms were observed externally, and only minimal rhizome discoloration was detected (Fig. 1d, h). Meanwhile, each hybrid demonstrated improved resistance compared to its corresponding maternal parent (Table 1, Fig. 1e-h).

In the field trials, symptoms of Fusarium wilt appeared in 'Baxijiao' and 'Jinyu' five months after planting. M. balbisiana and the hybrid 'Haifen No. 1' displayed noticeable yet mild external symptoms of Fusarium wilt during the dry and cold winter season of 2024. No external symptoms were observed in the other accessions throughout the duration of the field evaluation (Table 1). To confirm that Foc_TR4 was the causal agent of Fusarium wilt under field conditions, the nucleotide sequence of the pathogen was amplified from infected rhizome samples, as described in our previous study19. The results indicated that rhizome samples from 'Baxijiao', 'Jinyu', and M. balbisiana tested positive for Foc_TR4, those from 'Haifen No. 1' and M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis were occasionally positive, while samples from 'Yulin', 'Haijiao No. 1', and M. cheesmanii were generally negative.

Performance of hybrids of M. cheesmanii and Musa ABB cultivars
Crosses were made between two triploid cultivars ('Yulin' and 'Jinyu') and three diploid wild relatives (M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis, M. balbisiana, and M. cheesmanii), resulting in six unique combinations, which were evaluated for seed set (average number of seeds per fruit), seed germination percentage, offspring traits, and resistance to Foc_TR4 to assess their potential for banana breeding. The two triploid cultivars were female fertility identified in our previous study24. M. cheesmanii features a tall and black pseudo-stem (Fig. 2a), and crosses between 'Yulin'/'Jinyu' and M. cheesmanii displayed several outcomes (Table 2). Firstly, they showed the highest seed set (average number of seeds per fruit: 0.58±0.03). Secondly, the seed germination percentage was the lowest (≤ 1.7%), similar to that of the cross with M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis. Thirdly, the normal seedling (with healthy and regular appearance) percentage was moderate (slightly over 40%), being lower than that of the combinations with M. balbisiana but higher than those with M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis. Next, the offspring from these crosses exhibited the heaviest bunch weight among the three combinations with the same female parent; specifically, the offspring from the crosses between M. cheesmanii and 'Yulin' reached an average of 17.8 kg (significantly higher than the 10.0 kg and 13.5 kg observed with the other two male parents), and similarly, the offspring from the crosses between M. cheesmanii and 'Jinyu' showed an average bunch weight of 19.5 kg, outperforming the 13.5 kg and 16.1 kg recorded in the other combinations. In addition, the plant stature (defined as the ratio of plant girth to plant height) was the largest among the combinations with the same female parent; when 'Yulin' was used, the offspring from the cross with M. cheesmanii had a plant stature of 0.225, exceeding the 0.161 and 0.183 observed with M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis and M. balbisiana, respectively, while with 'Jinyu' the corresponding value was 0.171, slightly higher than the 0.167 and 0.163 seen with the other male parents, suggesting these plants may have relatively shorter, sturdier pseudo-stems that offer better resistance to wind damage and can support heavier bunches at maturity. Moreover, the majority of the offspring had red pseudo-stems, which were lighter than the deep black color of their male parent M. cheesmanii.

Significant heterobeltiosis was observed in the M. cheesmanii × 'Yulin' cross, with the hybrid showing complementary traits. First, it remained symptom-free when grown in Foc_TR4-infected fields (Table 1). Second, its bright red pseudo-stem provides additional ornament value (Fig. 2b,c). Third, its bunch weight was nearly double that of the maternal parent, with the hand arrangement resembling that of the paternal parent (Fig. 2d). Fourth, sensory evaluation showed that the hybrid fruit scored significantly higher than its maternal ABB cultivar for overall acceptability, indicating greater preference (Supplementary Table 1), while chemical composition analysis revealed significantly higher levels of β-carotene, soluble sugars, starch, carbohydrates, and sucrose (Supplementary Table 2), suggesting enhanced nutritional value and improved sweetness and overall eating quality. Fifth, it has an extended shelf-life of 6-10 days compared with 4-5 days for 'Yulin', with comparable fruit weight loss, slower softening of the pulp, and reduced malondialdehyde accumulation, supporting the observation that fruit quality remains largely unaffected despite peel blackening (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 3). Taken together, these results indicate that M. cheesmanii is cross compatible with certain cultivated bananas, yielding traits comparable to those of the two wild ancestors.

T2T gapless genome assembly and annotation of M. cheesmanii
The T2T gapless genome of M. cheesmanii was assembled by integrating PacBio high-fidelity (HiFi) reads, Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT) ultra-long reads, and Hi-C reads (Supplementary Table 4, 5). The estimated genome size was 438.13 Mb, with a heterozygosity rate of 0.432% (Supplementary Fig. 2a). The assembled T2T gap-free genome is 432.16 Mb in size, consisting of 11 pseudo-chromosomes (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Table 6), and accounts for 98.63% of the estimated genome. Quality assessment showed that 99.52% of the HiFi reads mapped to the genome, indicating high coverage and assembly accuracy. Additionally, the LTR assembly index (LAI) reached 11.64, further supporting the reliability of the assembly (Supplementary Fig. 2b). Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs (BUSCO) analysis revealed 98.57% completeness for the 1,614 core conserved genes of embryophyta, whereas k-mer based analyses yielded a QV score of 48.97 and completeness of 99.00%, respectively, both supporting the high quality of the genome (Supplementary Table 7, Supplementary Fig. 3). Hi-C interaction data also provided strong evidence for accurate chromosome ordering and orientation (Supplementary Fig. 4). Genome segment comparison showed that nearly all segments of the two AAB cultivars (Plantain and Silk)25 could not be assigned to the M. cheesmanii genome (Supplementary Fig. 5), consistent with the fact that this species has not previously been utilized in banana breeding programs.

Repetitive sequences make up 46.65% of the genome, including 41.96% transposable elements (TEs) and 4.69% tandem repeats (Supplementary Data 1). Gene annotation predicted 38,197 genes (Supplementary Table 5). Functional annotation showed that 39.43%, 39.14%, and 69.37% of genes were annotated in the GO (Gene Ontology), KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes), and Pfam databases, respectively, resulting in 77.31% of genes being functionally annotated (Supplementary Table 8). Telomeric repeat analysis identified eleven pairs of telomeres with repeat lengths ranging from 1,081 to 5,376 base pairs (Supplementary Table 9). All eleven centromeric regions were identified based on TEs, tandem repeats, and Nanica LINE (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Table 10).

Genome evolution and demographic history of Musa species
Phylogenomic analysis of 9,388 single-copy orthogroups from M. cheesmanii, Ensete glaucum, and five other Musa species (M. acuminata, M. balbisiana, M. schizocarpa, M. troglodytarum, and M. beccarii) revealed that the Musa section splits into two major clades, A and B (Fig. 3b). In total, 34,302 orthogroups were characterized from 254, 531 genes (Supplementary Table 11), among which 7,683 gene families showed significant expansion or contraction (P < 0.05). In M. cheesmanii, 381 gene families were significantly expanded and 481 contracted. The most significantly enriched biological processes were related to carbohydrate metabolism, sugar transport, post-transcriptional processing, and ribosome biogenesis (Supplementary Data 2), while contracted genes were mainly involved in plant development, photoperiodism, and stress response (Supplementary Data 3). Gene family expansions in clade B were most significantly enriched in carbohydrate metabolism and defense mechanisms, while contractions mainly affected plant development pathways (Supplementary Data 4, 5). Genes involved in sugar transport and glucose import were significantly expanded in the Musa section but contracted in the Callimusa section, highlighting key evolutionary divergence (Supplementary Data 6-9).

Genome size variation was noted between the two sections, with Callimusa genomes ranging from 570 Mb to 603 Mb, and Musa genomes from 432 Mb to 525 Mb26,27,28,29,30. The M. cheesmanii genome is 432.16 Mb, with 46.65% repetitive sequences, similar in size and TE content to M. balbisiana26, but more compact compared to other Musa species (M. acuminata: 468.82 Mb, TE: 49.78%27; M. schizocarpa: 496.92 Mb, TE: 53.04%28; M. beccarii: 569.64 Mb, TE: 55.99%29; M. troglodytarum: 603 Mb, TE: 59.62%30). The smaller genome sizes of clade B species, including M. cheesmanii, are likely due to the lower abundance of intact LTRs, primarily from Copia and Gypsy families, in M. cheesmanii and M. balbisiana compared to M. acuminata and M. schizocarpa (Supplementary Fig. 6).

In M. cheesmanii, at least two whole-genome duplication (WGD) events were identified, consistent with previous findings in Musa species, with no species-specific duplications observed. Our analysis revealed 29,016 duplicated genes in M. cheesmanii, including WGD-derived, tandem, proximal, transposed, and dispersed duplication events. Tandem duplications (TD) were more common in the Musa section, while proximal duplications (PD) predominated in Callimusa species (Supplementary Fig. 7). The retained WGD expanded genes were mainly involved in housekeeping processes, while the PD and TD expanded genes were primarily associated with sugar transport, including glucose, hexose, monosaccharide, carbohydrate, and proton transmembrane transport (Supplementary Fig. 8, Supplementary Data 10, 11). These findings highlight the role of WGD in stabilizing housekeeping functions and maintaining genome stability, while TD and PD duplications may have facilitated metabolic innovations and species-specific adaptations in the wild Musa species.

Over the past one million years, the Earth experienced approximately nine glacial-interglacial cycles31. Demographic history analysis indicates that the effective population sizes (Ne) of all four studied species in the Musa section underwent an initial expansion, followed by a subsequent decline (Fig. 3c). However, clades A (M. acuminata and M. schizocarpa) and B (M. balbisiana and M. cheesmanii) exhibited distinct population trajectories, with clade A undergoing more pronounced Ne fluctuations during glacial-interglacial cycles compared to clade B. The demographic histories of the two clade A species are nearly identical, with Ne peaking around 200,000 to 400,000 years ago, followed by a sharp decline. In contrast, the two clade B species reached their Ne peaks earlier, approximately 500,000 to 780,000 years ago, and subsequently experienced a more gradual decline. Before the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM, approximately 20,000 years ago32), the Ne of these species reached a plateau. However, during the LGM, clade A experienced a sharp decline, while clade B remained relatively stable in Ne.

Chromosomal rearrangement and structural variation in Musa species
Extensive chromosomal rearrangements, including fusions, fissions, and translocations, were mainly identified in the Callimusa section, consistent with its variable chromosome numbers (Fig. 3b). Fusion of chromosomes 8 and 9 in the Musa section formed chromosome 8 in M. troglodytarum. In M. beccarii, more fusion and fissions events were observed. Between M. beccarii and M. troglodytarum, 135 syntenic blocks comprising 55,342 gene pairs were detected, with over half (77/135) scattered across different chromosomes (Fig. 3b). In contrast, the Musa section exhibited fewer rearrangements, though many occurred at hotpot regions overlapping with structural variation sites in the Callimusa section (e.g., chromosomes 1, 3, and 5). M. cheesmanii shared most conserved syntenic blocks with M. balbisiana and M. acuminata, except for a few translocations and inversions (Supplementary Fig. 9). No large chromosomal rearrangement was detected between M. schizocarpa and M. acuminata. Two major structural variations were identified in the Musa section: an inversion on chromosome 5 and a large reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 1 and 3 (Supplementary Fig. 9). Specifically, the chromosome 5 inversion was observed only in M. acuminata and M. schizocarpa, while the translocation between chromosomes 1 and 3 occurred between M. balbisiana and other Musa species studied. The read alignments around the breakpoints of these structural variations supported their existence (Supplementary Fig. 10).

Genome-wide survey of resistance genes
A genome-wide survey of R genes across M. cheesmanii, M. balbisiana, and M. acuminata was conducted, identifying 476 loci containing NB-ARC (Nucleotide-binding site) and LRR (Leucine-rich repeats) domains (NLR). Functional enrichments of these NLRs across the representative genomes consistently highlighted plant-microbe interactions, immune response, and defense-related pathways, supporting the robustness of R gene annotation (Supplementary Fig. 11). These NLR loci were classified into RESISTANCE TO POWDERY MILDEW 8-like coiled-coil NLRs (RNL), coiled-coil NLRs (CNL), and other NLRs33, whereas Toll/interleukin 1 receptor-like NLRs (TNL) were absent in banana. Among these categories, RNLs were the most abundant, accounting for 77.50%-83.64% of the total NLRs in each genome. Phylogenetic relationships of these NLRs and lineage-specific expansions and diversification events were presented in Fig. 4a. Orthogroup analysis revealed copy number variation of R genes between M. cheesmanii and M. balbisiana, as well as within M. acuminata (Fig. 4a, b). Some large translocations encompass multiple R gene clusters, such as the translocation involving chromosomes 1 and 3 between M. balbisiana and other Musa species, and the previously reported large reciprocal translocation involving 3 Mb and 10 Mb from chromosomes 1 and 4 within M. acuminata34 (Fig. 4c). In parallel, certain orthogroups, including OG0000000 and OG0000011, have shifted their chromosomal locations, reflecting similar patterns of genomic rearrangement (Fig. 4b). Moreover, many R genes were co-localized with transposable elements, suggesting a potential role of TEs in R gene family expansion and divergence (Supplementary Fig. 12).

Polymorphisms of eBSV integrants and RGA2
Banana streak virus (BSV), a pararetrovirus in the genus Badnavirus (Caulimoviridae), is approximately 7 kb in length with a double-stranded DNA genome comprising three consecutive open-reading frames (ORFs)35,36. To assess the suitability of M. cheesmanii as a male parent in banana hybrid breeding, endogenous BSV (eBSV) sequences were examined and compared with those in M. balbisiana. Initially, potential eBSV loci were investigated in the sect. Musa species, including M. acuminata, M. schizocarpa, M. balbisiana, and M. cheesmanii. No large viral sequences insertions were observed in M. acuminata and M. schizocarpa, with most blast hits fragment around 540 bp. In contrast, full-length BSV insertions were detected in M. balbisiana, such as two distinct BSV: banana streak IM virus (BSImV) and banana streak Mysore virus (BSMysV) sequences located on chromosome 2 (Supplementary Fig. 13a). However, M. cheesmanii harbored only large fragmental integrants, including three eBSV-like insetions regions: eBSV-like 1 on chromosome 5 (42,273,844-42,282,239 bp), eBSV-like 2 on chromosome 1 (6,376,588-6,396,669 bp), and eBSV-like 3 on chromosome 3 (15,045,005-15,056,027 bp). Phylogenetic analysis indicated their origin from a mixed subgroup containing isolate of BSV on a cultivar in Yunnan (BSAcYuV), a cultivar in Vietnam (BSAcVnV), and BSImV, which was distinct from M. balbisiana (Fig. 5a). Compared with the complete genome of BSAcYuV, the ORFs of the potential eBSV in M. cheesmanii were highly fragmented and rearranged (Fig. 5b-d). The eBSV-like 1 (Fig. 5b) and eBSV-like 3 (Fig. 5d) were relatively intact but lacked ORFI and had interrupted ORFIII due to stop codon insertions. Additionally, the viral integrants in M. cheesmanii diverged from the reference BSAcYuV with an overall similarity of around 80%, compared to more than 99% similarity to BSImV and BSMysV in M. balbisiana. Consistent with the genome sequences, the eBSV-like transcripts in M. cheesmanii were fragmented, whereas in M. balbisiana, these regions were generally expressed as complete transcripts (Supplementary Figs. 13b and 14).

It has been reported that introducing RGA2, a gene isolated from M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis, into Cavendish conferred resistance to Foc_TR4, with transgenic plants remaining disease-free over a three-year field trial37. This RGA2 gene consists of a single exon, and its ORF is 3,699 bp in length. To investigate its genetic variation, the ORF of RGA2 was compared across M. acuminata, M. balbisiana, M. cheesmanii, and 'Baxijiao'. In total, 166 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were identified, approximately 57% of which were nonsynonymous mutations. A 6-bp insertion was identified at position 1,570 bp (site 1, Fig. 5e) in M. balbisiana and M. cheesmanii, potentially specific to B-lineage species. At 3,687 bp (site 2, Fig. 5e), a T-to-A mutation resulting in a premature stop codon was found in M. balbisiana and in two RGA2 homologs of 'Baxijiao' but not in M. cheesmanii. This mutation resulted in a truncated peptide chain with loss of six amino acids and subtle structural changes in the LRR domain, which is essential for pathogen recognition and signal modulation, altering β-sheet orientation and loop length (Supplementary Fig. 15). The nonsense mutation was confirmed by HiFi read alignments (Supplementary Fig. 16).

Transcriptomic and metabolic analyses reveal insights into pseudo-stem coloration in Musa species
To investigate the mechanisms underlying pseudo-stem coloration, comparative transcriptomic and metabolic analyses were conducted across Musa species: M. acuminata (green pseudo-stem, Mac), M. balbisiana (green pseudo-stem, Mba), and M. cheesmanii (green top pseudo-stem, Mch; black main pseudo-stem, Mchb). Principal component analysis (PCA) and transcriptional expression heatmap across species revealed significant transcriptomic differences, with good reproducibility among replicates (Supplementary Fig. 17a). While Mch and Mchb exhibited slight differences, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) analysis identified 7,098, 6,030, and 3,723 DEGs in comparisons of Mac vs. Mchb, Mba vs. Mchb, and Mch vs. Mchb, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 18). A total of 289, 314, and 338 genes in the phenylpropanoid (map00940), flavonoid (map00941), and anthocyanin biosynthesis (map00942) pathways were identified in M. cheesmanii, M. balbisiana, and M. acuminata, respectively (Supplementary Data 12-14). Besides, a total of 34 genes encoding polyphenol oxidase (PPO), peroxidase (POD), and DOPA decarboxylase (DDC) were identified (Fig. 6a). The expression patterns of these genes were then compared across the three species. Among these, 41 genes were up-regulated in Mch or Mchb (Supplementary Fig. 17b). Further pairwise comparisons of green (Mac, Mba, Mch) vs. black (Mchb) pseudo-stems identified 66, 50, and 44 DEGs. Only three genes were consistently up-regulated in Mchb and reflected the expression patterns observed across the three species: mch1s9g00634 (CCoAOMT), mch1s9g00701 (BGLU26), and mch1s2g02531 (PAL2) (Supplementary Fig. 19). Then additional comparisons based on mean-transformed expression were made between black and green pseudo-stems to focus on more anthocyanins-related structural genes (Supplementary Fig. 17b). Four flavonoid and anthocyanin biosynthesis genes, CHS (mch1s10g01364), FLS3 (mch1s10g02760), FE3'H (mch1s7g03161), and UFGT (mch1s10g02996), were up-regulated in the black pseudo-stem (Mchb) of M. cheesmanii across all replicate comparisons. We further performed quantitative RT-PCR (qPCR) to validate the expression of the seven identified genes in green and black pseudo-stems of M. cheesmanii. Two genes (BGLU26 and PAL2) failed to amplify, F3'H showed higher expression in black pseudo-stems but not significantly, while the remaining four genes were significantly up-regulated in black pseudo-stems (Supplementary Fig. 20). These four genes (CCoAOMT, CHS, FLS3, and UFGT) are therefore considered key candidates contributing to the black coloration of M. cheesmanii pseudo-stems (Fig. 6b). In addition, we performed qPCR analysis of F3'5'H, a key gene involved in the delphinidin-based pathway (Fig. 6a), and found that F3'5'H expression was elevated in the black pseudo-stem of M. cheesmanii (Supplementary Fig. 20). Among 3,498 identified transcription factors (TFs) in M. cheesmanii, 250 bHLH, 251 MYB/MYB-related, and 111 bZIP candidates were found (Supplementary Data 15-17). Further analysis identified 12 TFs consistently differentially expressed in Mchb, with 8 up-regulated and 4 down-regulated, including bHLH, MYB, and bZIP factors. Moreover, species-level comparisons (Mac vs. Mchb and Mba vs. Mchb) identified 6 transcription factors linked to light responses from a total of 37 identified, accounting for approximately 16% (Supplementary Fig. 21).

A total of 66 anthocyanin metabolites were identified across the three species, and the heatmap of hierarchical cluster analysis showed substantial differences (Supplementary Fig. 22). Among these metabolites, 3 belong to the pelargonidin-based pathway, while 27 and 29 are part of the cyanidin-based and delphinidin-based pathways, respectively. Most of these metabolites were much more abundant in M. acuminata (Supplementary Fig. 22), likely because it belongs to clade A and is more distantly related to M. cheesmanii. Therefore, we focused on comparing metabolite levels between black and green pseudo-stems of clade B species. We selected the top 10 most abundant metabolites in the black pseudo-stem (Mchb) of M. cheesmanii for comparison. Among them, six metabolites showed significantly higher abundances in Mchb than in the green pseudo-stems (Mch and Mba) (Fig. 6c). Two procyanidins (colorless or pale flavonoids) were the most abundant. Although they are known to polymerize into dark pigments through enzymes such as PPO or POD, transcriptome data revealed no significant up-regulation of PPO or POD genes in Mchb (Supplementary Fig. 19), suggesting that the role of procyanidins in pseudo-stem blackening is unclear. The remaining four metabolites were Delphinidin-3-O-rutinoside, Petunidin-3-O-rutinoside, Delphinidin-3-O-glucoside, and Petunidin-3-O-glucoside, all belonging to the delphinidin-based pathway, indicating that this pathway plays an important role in the black coloration of M. cheesmanii pseudo-stems.

## Methods

Plant materials
Plant materials were collected from M. cheesmanii, which is conserved at South China Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences, under the accession code ge-lz-013. The plant originated from South Himalaya (Medog, China), obtained in 2019. Currently, it is maintained in a greenhouse in Guangzhou, China, where it is actively monitored and utilized for ongoing breeding and genomic studies.

Fusarium wilt resistance evaluation
Eight accessions were selected for resistance testing. They included three wild banana relatives (M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis, M. balbisiana, and M. cheesmanii), two banana cultivars belonging to the ABB group ('Jinyu', Pisang Awak group, and 'Yulin', Dajiao group), their respective hybrids with M. cheesmanii ('Haifen No. 1' and 'Haijiao No. 1'), and a susceptible control, the Cavendish cultivar 'Baxijiao' (AAA). The M. cheesmanii accession was germinated from seeds collected in Medog, China, while the other seven accessions were propagated via tissue culture from plants grown at South China Botanical Garden or Guangxi Minzu University. Plantlets were grown in pots containing disinfected Tref substrates (Jiffy, Moerdijk, Netherlands). During the acclimatization period, the plants were watered daily and weekly supplemented with 50 mL per plant of Murashige and Skoog’s solution to promote healthy growth.

Greenhouse evaluations were carried out in 2024 under controlled conditions, with temperatures ranging from 26-35 °C and approximately 85% relative humidity. The strain used for testing was Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense tropical race 4 (Foc_TR4, VCG01216). Briefly, for each accession, twenty-one plantlets with similar morphological characteristics (6-7 leaves and 30-50 cm in height) were selected. Fifteen plantlets were individually inoculated by pouring aliquots (2 mL per aliquot) of spore suspension (5 × 106 spores mL-1) directly into five equidistant holes around the plant base near the rhizome; the others treated with sterile water were kept as controls. The whole experiment was replicated three times.

Field evaluations were conducted at an experimental plot in Nanning, Guangxi province (22°48’ N, 108°22’ E; Alt. 106 m), which was naturally infested with Foc_TR4, from 2023 to 2025 (including three replicates). Briefly, fifteen acclimatized plants (40-50 cm in height) of each accession were planted in a randomized block design. Plants were supplied monthly with 50-150 mL of Murashige and Skoog solution per plant, depending on their developmental stage, and were watered weekly.

Fusarium wilt resistance was evaluated using several parameters, starting with the incubation period (IP), which refers to the average time (in days after inoculation, dai) between inoculation and the appearance of symptoms in greenhouse conditions. Disease incidence was measured by calculating the proportion of plants showing both external and internal Fusarium wilt symptoms relative to the total number of plants assessed. In addition, disease severity was evaluated and the disease index (DI) was determined by examining external symptoms and rhizome discoloration (internal symptom) according to Li et al.19. Briefly, disease severity of both external and internal symptoms were deemed according to the respective scale of 0-3. The DI was calculated as:
∑(score in the scale × frequency)
𝐷𝐼 = × 100 (1)
total number of plants × maximum class in the scale
In greenhouse, IP was assessed by visual inspection of initial external appearance of symptoms every 2 days starting 7 dai; internal symptoms were evaluated visually when a plantlet died or at the end of the experiments (65 dai). In field, evaluations of external disease intensity (incidence and severity) were performed every 2 weeks; when the plant showed serious symptom or at the end of the experiment (21 months after planting), internal symptoms (rhizome discoloration) were evaluated.

Cross-compatibility evaluation
Crosses were made between two triploid cultivars (female parents) and three diploid wild relatives (male parents), resulting in six unique combinations (Table 2). The two female parents used in the crosses were 'Yulin' (Musa ABB Dajiao group) and 'Jinyu' (Musa ABB Pisang Awak group). The Dajiao group is favored in South China, whereas the Pisang Awak group is widely popular in Southeast Asia and ranks as the second most consumed banana variety in China after Cavendish. Both cultivars are known for their low fertility. 'Yulin' and 'Jinyu', the representative cultivars of these two groups, were both grown at Guangxi Minzu University. The three male parents, M. acuminata ssp. malaccensis, M. balbisiana, and M. cheesmanii, were the same as those used in the Fusarium wilt resistance evaluation section. Each female parent was artificially crossed with each of the three male parents, resulting in a total of six crosses.

Artificial crossings were carried out continuously from 2022 onward. For each cross, pollen grains were carefully harvested from the male parent and transferred onto the receptive flowers of the female parent in the field. To prevent any accidental contamination from foreign pollen, the emerging female flowers and male pollen sources were carefully bagged. After the seeds were harvested, they were germinated in vitro to develop an F1 progeny population for each of the six combinations. The seedlings were then acclimated in a controlled greenhouse environment before being transplanted into a field naturally infested with Foc_TR4 to assess their resistance.

The seed set (average number of seeds per fruit), seed germination percentage, and several key morphological traits of the offspring, including normal seedling (with healthy and regular appearance) rate, bunch weight, pseudo-stem height, plant stature (defined as pseudo-stem girth at 150 cm above ground to the total height of the pseudo-stem when flowering), and pseudo-stem color, were evaluated to assess the cross-compatibility of the different combinations. Seed set, germination, and seedling architecture were evaluated using >3000 fruits, >300 seeds, and >80 progenies (each with three replicates). Pseudo-stem color was visually assessed in >100 plants, while bunch weight, pseudo-stem height, and plant stature were measured from ten parental plants and ten selected hybrid lines (five plants per line). These traits were critical for understanding the potential of each cross to contribute to banana breeding efforts, particularly in terms of disease resistance and other agronomically important characteristics.

To evaluate heterobeltiosis in agronomic traits, fruit quality was assessed for 'Yulin' and its hybrid 'Haijiao No. 1' ('Yulin' × M. cheesmanii). The evaluation included sensory assessment, chemical composition analysis, and shelf-life determination. For sensory evaluation, blind tests were conducted. Twenty-six panelists without oral diseases tasted fully ripe fruits from both cultivars and independently scored them on eight parameters: sweetness, acidity, banana aroma, texture, astringency, off-flavor, overall flavor, and overall acceptability. For chemical composition analysis, the ripe pulps of each cultivar were analyzed for sixteen parameters following the corresponding GB/T (National Recommended Standard of the People’s Republic of China) or NY/T (National Standard of Agricultural Industry of the People’s Republic of China) methods (Supplementary Table 2). For shelf-life assessment, fruits were stored at room temperatures, specifically from 32 °C at day to 24 °C at night. Shelf-life was monitored every two days by photographic documentation, sensory evaluation, and postharvest quality (including fruit weight loss, pulp firmness, and malondialdehyde content), starting from the end of the green-life stage (when the peel begins to yellow) until the end of the edible period. Weight loss rate was calculated as:
