Pulp firmness and malondialdehyde content were tested following NY/T 2009-2011 and GB5009.181-216, respectively. For each cultivar, three biological replicates were used, each consisting of three fruits.

Genome sequencing
Fresh young leaves of M. cheesmanii were collected, immediately stored in liquid nitrogen, and then sent to BGI (Shenzhen, China) for genome sequencing. The CTAB method49 was used to isolate the total genomic DNA from the leaves. For PE150 (paired-end 150 bp) sequencing, libraries with an insertion size of 350 bp were constructed and sequenced on a DNBseq platform. The raw PE150 reads were then filtered using Fastp v0.23.250 with default parameters, generating 47.13 Gb of clean PE150 reads (Supplementary Table 4). PacBio HiFi sequencing was carried out on a Sequel II platform, yielding 38.39 Gb of clean HiFi reads after filtering with Fastp using the parameters: (-q 20 -l 1000 -A) (Supplementary Table 4). ONT sequencing was carried out on a PromethION platform. After filtration with Fastp with the parameters: (-q 7 -u 100 -e 7 -A -l 40000), 114.43 Gb of ONT clean reads longer than 40 kb were generated (Supplementary Table 4). Hi-C libraries were prepared by formaldehyde cross-linking, DpnII digestion, biotin labeling, proximity ligation, purification, and size selection, followed by sequencing on the DNBseq platform with PE150 reads. Finally, 139.81 Gb of Hi-C clean reads were produced after filtration using Fastp (Supplementary Table 4). For RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), total RNA from leaves and roots was extracted and sequenced on the DNBseq platform in the PE150 pattern. A total of 14.44 Gb of clean RNA reads were obtained after filtration using Fastp (Supplementary Table 4).

Genome survey and high-quality genome assembly
Based on HiFi reads, Jellyfish v2.3.051 was utilized to calculate k-mers of 17, 21, and 31, and the outputs were subjected to GenomeScope252 to assess genome size and heterozygosity. Hifiasm v0.19.353 was applied to assemble the HiFi reads with the parameter (--ul) to integrate the ONT reads. The generated preliminary assembled heterozygous contigs (p_ctg) were subjected to two rounds of polishing using NextPolish v1.4.154 with HiFi reads. Redundant contigs caused by heterozygosity were then eliminated using Purge_Haplotigs v1.1.255. Subsequently, the Hi-C clean reads were aligned to the purged genome assembly using BWA v0.7.1756, followed by Juicer v1.657 to identify valid interaction pairs. Finally, 3D-DNA v20100858 was used to anchor the final contigs into pseudo-chromosomes, and Juicebox Assembly Tools v1.11.0859 was used to manually improve the accuracy of the chromosomal assembly. Then, HiCExplorer v3.060 was used to visualize the Hi-C data.

To further improve genome quality, TGS-GapCloser v1.2.161 was applied to fill the remaining four gaps in the pseudo-chromosomes using the assembled ONT contigs generated from NextDenovo v2.5.0 (https://github.com/Nextomics/NextDenovo). The reliability of gap-filling sequences was validated by examing breakpoints using long-read alignments and Hi-C contact data (Supplementary Figs 23, 24). With each terminal 100 kb sequences as probes, minimap2 v2.2462 was performed against polished HiFi primary contig database for telomere repairing. Finally, a T2T gapless genome was generated after polished by NextPolish with HiFi reads. The mapping rate of final assembly was evaluated using SAMtools v1.1463. To monitor quality changes across different assembly stages, BUSCO v5.4.364, Merqury v1.365, and KAT v2.4.266 were employed for genome quality assessment. Overall, although polishing appeared to slightly lower the quality of the assembly, the results demonstrated consistently high-quality assemblies at every stage (Supplementary Table 7). The R package Rideogram67 was used to visualize and map genome-wide data on the ideograms based on 1-Mb windows.

To assess the potential contribution of M. cheesmanii to banana cultivars, we analyzed Plantain and Silk (AAB cultivars)25 using chromosome painting68 with multiple ancestral genome assemblies, including five M. acuminata subspecies (malaccensis, banksii, zebrina, burmannica, and halabanensis)9,27, M. schizocarpa28, M. balbisiana26, and M. cheesmanii, for segment comparisons.

Genome assembly annotation
Telomeric and centromeric regions were identified using quarTeT69. Using the repeat monomer AAATCCC/TTTAGGG, TeloExplorer (Module #3) was performed to identify telomeric regions, and TIDK v0.2.1 (https://github.com/tolkit/telomeric-identifier) was used to explore and search telomeric regions through automatic workflows. CentroMiner (Module #4) was utilized to predict centromere candidates using transposable element annotation in GFF3 format and a genome FASTA file as input. Based on period and copy number, centromeric tandem repeat monomers were screened, clustered to reduce redundancy, and aligned to corresponding chromosomes (Supplementary Table 10). The Nanica LINE reported in M. acuminata70 was downloaded (https://banana-genome-hub.southgreen.fr/node/50/353) as a probe for further checking the centromeric region in the M. cheesmanii genome, and blastn v2.11.071 was applied to perform searches.

Extensive de novo TE Annotator (EDTA) v2.1.072 was employed to discover TEs with the parameters: (--species others --step all --evaluate 1 --sensitive 1 --anno 1). The non-redundant TE library yielded by EDTA was then imported into RepeatMasker v4.1.073 to soft-mask repeat sequences in the genome using the parameter “-xsmall”. In addition, Tandem Repeats Finder v4.0974 was employed to identify tandem repeats. For comparative analysis of TE contents, the EDTA pipeline with identical parameters was used to annotate other Musa species. LTR_retriever v2.9.075 was used to extract intact LTR retrotransposons and calculate their insertion time within Musa species using a mutation rate of 1.3e-8 from the monocot species rice.

The standard MAKER3 v3.01.033876 pipeline was utilized to annotate gene structures. For homology prediction, all high-confidence protein sequences were imported from the Swiss-Prot database77, and raw gene structures were predicted based on tblastn alignments. The RNA-seq data were mapped to the T2T genome using HISAT2 v2.2.178, and genome-guided transcripts were obtained by StringTie v2.1.779. Then, AUGUSTUS v3.3.2 and SNAP v20131129 were employed to train the best predicted gene models. The MAKER3 pipeline was run twice to obtain more complete gene annotations. Finally, eggNOG mapper80 was used to functionally annotate the predicted coding genes based on the eggNOG v5.0 database81.

Comparative phylogenomics
Orthologous gene families were clustered using the longest transcripts from M. cheesmanii and six other Musaceae species, downloaded from the Banana Genome Hub (https://banana-genome-hub.southgreen.fr/)26,27,28,29,30,82,83. The remaining six species include three from the sect. Musa (M. acuminata, M. schizocarpa and M. balbisiana), two from the sect. Callimusa (M. troglodytarum and M. beccarii), and the outgroup, Ensete glaucum. Orthofinder v2.5.484 was employed to classify the gene families. Orthologous sequences were aligned using MAFFT v7.51585, trimmed using trimAl v1.2rev5986, and then concatenated. Phylogenetic tree was constructed using RAxML-NG v1.187. FigTree v1.4.4 (https://github.com/rambaut/figtree) was used to visualize the phylogenetic tree. MCScan88 was utilized to identify structural variations with the parameters: (--cscore .99, --minspan 30). Then, CAFE v589 was utilized to simulate the dynamics of orthologous gene family expansion and contraction. TBtools v2.04290 was used to perform GO enrichment analysis for significantly expanded and contracted gene families in M. cheesmanii. Hypergeometric tests combined with and the Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) method were applied to obtain adjusted P values, retaining only GO terms with a BH adjustment P < 0.05. The GO enrichment results were visualized using ChiPlot (https://www.chiplot.online/).

Whole-genome duplication and structure variation
WGDI91 was introduced to identify whole-genome duplications (WGDs) in M. cheesmanii and six other Musaceae species26,27,28,29,30,82. Protein sequences were subjected to all-against-all and inter-specific comparisons using BLASTP v2.13.0 in the BLAST package71 with the parameters: (-outfmt 6 -evalue 1e-5 -num_alignments 20). MCScan88 was employed to establish collinearity between gene pairs, filtering out non-collinear gene pairs and tandem duplicated genes. Then, MUSCLE92 was used to align the proteins. The MCScan python version was used to identify syntenic blocks among these Musaceae assemblies with the parameters: (--cscore .99, --minspan 30). DupGen-finder93 was used to identify various types of duplicated genes in these Musaceae species including WGDs, tandem duplications (TDs), proximal duplications (PDs), transposed duplications (TRDs), and dispersed duplications (DSDs). GEO enrichment analysis was conducted using TBtools v2.04290 on 583 expanded genes derived from TD and PD events. Significant GO terms were visualized using ChiPlot (https://www.chiplot.online/).

Estimation of demographic history in the Musa section
Paired-end reads of three Musa A-clade/B-clade species26,27,28, along with M. cheesmanii sequenced in this study, were mapped to the assembled genome using the BWA-MEM algorithm56. SAMtools v1.1063 was used to remove duplicate and unpaired error-mapped reads from the alignments. Then, mpileup was performed in BCFtools94 with the parameters: (-Ou -I), and variant calling was conducted using BCFtools with the parameters: (-c -Ov). The vcf2fq in vcfutils.pl with the parameters (-d 10 -D 100) was used to convert the consensus genotype from VCF to FASTQ format. Next, the evolutionary effective population size of the four sect. Musa species was inferred using the Pairwise Sequentially Markovian Coalescent (PSMC, https://github.com/lh3/psmc) model with the parameters: (-N25 -t15 -r5 -p ‘4+25*2+4+6’ ). The PSMC results were scaled using a generation time of 1 year and a mutation rate of 1.3e-8.

Resistance gene analysis
Resistance (R) genes across M. cheesmanii, M. balbisiana, and M. acuminata (MAv4, MAH1, MAH2) were identified using the FindPlantNLRs pipeline v2.033, which predicts loci containing NB-ARC and LRR domains from unmasked genome assemblies. To remove false positives, both the prediction and annotation stages were integrated. Orthogroups of R genes were inferred based on protein sequence similarity using OrthoFinder v2.5.484. Multiple sequence alignments were generated with MAFFT v7.52685 under default parameters and trimmed with trimAI v1.5.rev086 under -automated1 mode to remove non-conserved sites. Maximum likelihood phylogenetic inference was conducted using IQ-TREE v 2.4.095 with the best-fit model JTT+F+R6 and 1000 bootstrap. Phylogenetic trees were visualized with iTOL v796. GO enrichment analysis for R genes in each species was performed using TBtools v2.04290 (Significant at BH adjustment P < 0.05 level).

eBSV integrants
Available reference banana streak virus (BSV) and endogenous BSV (eBSV) sequences (DQ092436.1, KJ013508.1, AY750155.1, AY493509.1, ENC_003381.1, NC_006955.1) were downloaded from GenBank or NCBI database70,97,98. BLAST analysis for M. acuminata, M. schizocarpa, M. balbisiana, and M. cheesmanii was performed using full-length of BSV and eBSV or partial cds fragment of the ORFIII like region as described by D'Hont et al.70. Alignment regions with <500 bp length and <75% identity percentage were filtered. Then, in order to check whether complete eBSV integration exists, consecutive loci with alignment length exceeding 1,000 bp were focused on. Sequences were further extracted from the 2 kb upstream of the first alignment locus and the 2 kb downstream of the last one. Manual annotation and sequence codon frequency statistics were performed using Geneious Prime 2022.2.2 (https://www.geneious.com) with interior ORFs included and a 300 bp minimum size for finding ORFs. Reorganization with duplications and inversions was checked again by BLAST with E-value set as 1e-5 and visualized by TBtools90. Only BSV sequences with full-length and extracted consecutive regions were used to obtain a more reliable BSV phylogeny. All nucleotide sequences were aligned using MAFFT85 and then alignments were trimmed using trimAl86. Phylogenetic tree was constructed using IQ-TREE v2.3.695 with best-fit model TPM2u+F+R3 and 100 bootstraps.

RGA2 polymorphisms
RGA2 sequence was downloaded from GenBank (accession numbers EU616673)99. BLAST analysis for cultivar 'Baxijiao', M. acuminata, M. balbisiana, and M. cheesmanii was performed using RGA2 sequence as reference. The 1 kb upstream and downstream regions of the hit loci were extracted and examined for annotation and correction. All orthologous RGA2 sequences were aligned using ClustalW algorithm for DNA sequences and MUSCLE algorithm for protein sequences in MEGA11100. AlphaFold3101 was used to predict protein structures.

Transcriptome analysis of pseudo-stem in the Musa genus
To investigate why M. cheesmanii exhibits black color in its pseudo-stem, transcriptome analysis was performed on pseudo-stem samples from four groups (three replicates each): M. acuminata (Mac), M. balbisiana (Mba), and M. cheesmanii (group Mch/Mchb). For M. cheesmanii, samples were collected from the top pseudo-stem (green, Mch) and the main pseudo-stem (black, Mchb). For the other two species, samples were collected from the main pseudo-stem (green color). Total RNAs extracted from these pseudo-stems were sequenced on the DNBseq platform in the PE150 pattern. Subsequently, raw reads were trimmed and filtered using Fastp v0.23.250. Clean RNA-seq reads were then mapped to the assembled M. cheesmanii genome using HISAT2 v2.2.178, and raw counts were quantified using featureCounts v2.0 .4102. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between any two groups were identified using DESeq2103 with criteria set as |log2FoldChange| ≥ 1.0 and adjusted P ≤ 0.05. Besides, normalization expression level was calculated by transcripts per million (TPM) for convenient direct comparisons of all sampled groups. Based on transcriptomic data, functional annotation, and KEGG pathways (http://www.kegg.jp/kegg/pathway.html), candidate genes involved in phenylpropanoid biosynthesis (map00940), flavonoid biosynthesis (map00941), and anthocyanin biosynthesis (map00942) were identified in M. cheesmanii, M. balbisiana, and M. acuminata. Plant transcription factors (TFs), transcriptional regulators (TRs), and protein kinases (PKs) were identified using the iTAK program104. MYB, bHLH, and bZIP type key families of TFs, known for their roles in regulating anthocyanin biosynthesis, were identified.

Quantitative RT-PCR
For the qPCR quantification of pigmentation-related genes, the total RNAs were extracted from the green and black pseudo-stems of M. cheesmanii (Mch and Mchb). The extracted RNAs were reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the HiScript II 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (+gDNA wiper) according to the manufacturer’s protocol, and the resulting cDNA was subsequently diluted with 100 μL of RNase-free ddH2O. The specific primers used for amplification were synthesized using standard phosphoramidite chemistry and purified by polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (Wuhan Tianyi Huayu Gene Technology Co., Ltd, China), and the sequences were listed in Supplementary Table 12. All data were collected from three biological replicates. The reaction system (20 μL) contained ChamQ Blue Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix, 10 μL; 10 μM Primer 1, 0.4 μL; 10 μM Primer 2, 0.4 μL; cDNA, 2.2 μL; ddH2O, 7 μL. PCR cycles were 95 °C 5 m; 95 °C 10 s, 60 °C 30 s, 40 cycles. Relative mRNA level for each gene was calculated by 2-ΔΔCT methods with L2 set as reference gene105,106.

Anthocyanin metabolomic analysis
The pseudo-stem samples from M. acuminata (Mac), M. balbisiana (Mba), and M. cheesmanii (Mch/Mchb) were randomly collected in the South China Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences (three biological replicates for each group, total n = 12). The samples were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, ground to powder (50 mg for each replicate) followed by freeze-dried, and stored at -80 °C. Subsequently, the dried tissues were extracted twice using 0.5 mL methanol/water/hydrochloric acid (500:500:1, v/v/v), followed by vortexing (5 min), ultrasonication (5 min), and centrifugation (12,000 g, 4 °C, 3 min). Supernatants were pooled and filtered through 0.22 μm membranes for LC-MS/MS analysis.

The sample extracts were analyzed using an UPLC-ESI-MS/MS system (UPLC, ExionLCTM AD, http://sciex.com.cn/; MS, Applied Biosystems 6500 Triple Quadrupole, https://sciex.com.cn/). Chromatographic separation was performed on a Waters ACQUITY BEH C18 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7 μm) using a UPLC system with mobile phase A consisting of water (0.1% formic acid) and mobile phase B consisting of methanol (0.1% formic acid). The gradient elution program was set as follows: 95:5 V/V at 0 min, 50:50 V/V at 6 min, 5:95 V/V at 12 min, held for 2 min, 95:5 V/V at 14 min, held for 2 min. The flow rate was at 0.35 mL/min, the column temperature was maintained at 40 °C, and the injection volume was 2 μL.

Detection was performed on a QTRAP® 6500+ LC-MS/MS system in positive ESI mode with scheduled multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). The ESI source parameters were set as follows: ion spray voltage, 5500 V; source temperature, 550 °C; curtain gas, 35 psi. For each analyte, declustering potential (DP) and collision energy (CE) were individually optimized, and a compound-specific set of MRM transitions was monitored within defined retention-time windows according to chromatographic elution.

Metabolite quantification was performed using a triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (QTRAP® 6500+) in Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) mode. In MRM, the first quadrupole (Q1) selects the precursor ion of the target metabolite, filtering out non-target ions to reduce interference. The precursor ion is fragmented in the collision cell (Q2), and the third quadrupole (Q3) selectively monitors a characteristic fragment ion, improving quantitative accuracy and reproducibility. Chromatographic peak areas of target metabolites were integrated for all samples and converted to concentrations using external calibration curves. Standard stock solutions (1 mg/mL in 50% MeOH) were diluted to working concentrations of 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 2000, and 5000 ng/mL. Peak areas of standards were plotted against concentrations to generate calibration curves, which were used to calculate metabolite concentrations in samples. The final metabolite content (μg/g) in each sample was calculated as:
Metabolite content = c × V × 10−6 (3)
m
where c is the concentration derived from the calibration curve (ng/mL), V is the extraction volume (μL), and m is the sample mass (g).

Mass spectrometry data were processed using Analyst v1.6.3 (SCIEX, Framingham, MA), and peak integration and quantification were carried out using MultiQuant v3.0.3 (SCIEX, Framingham, MA). Total ion chromatograms (TIC) and extracted ion chromatograms (XIC) were used to visualize metabolite detection profiles and verify peak quality. Authentic standards were used when available, whereas compounds lacking purified standards were semi-quantified using class-based calibration. The corresponding standards, calibration curves, and quantification mode for each compound are provided in Supplementary Data 18.

PCA and OPLS-DA were performed for multivariate analysis to explore metabolite variation patterns between groups (biological replicates ≥3). VIP values from OPLS-DA combined with univariate P-value/FDR and FoldChange were used to identify significantly differential metabolites. Hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) results of both samples and metabolites are presented as heatmaps with dendrograms. HCA was carried out with the R package Pheatmap, where normalized signal intensities of metabolites (Z-score normalization) are visualized as a color spectrum. Significantly differentially expressed metabolites between groups were determined based on criteria of |log2FoldChange| ≥ 1.0 and P ≤ 0.05. The ten most abundant metabolites in the black pseudo-stem (Mchb) of M. cheesmanii were selected for comparison with those in green pseudo-stems. Two-sided Student’s t-test analysis was further included for six target metabolites.

Statistics and reproducibility
Field experiment data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Duncan’s multiple range test, with differences considered significant at P < 0.05. For omics analyses (transcriptome and metabolomics) and qPCR experiments, three biological replicates were included. Statistical significance was assessed using a two-sided Student’s t-test at P < 0.05 (*), P < 0.01 (**), P < 0.001 (***). For comparative analysis of metabolite composition between Musa species, two phylogenetically closely related species were selected. No statistical method was employed to predetermine sample size, and all data were included in the analyses without exclusion.

### Reviewer 3

Review of Manuscript ID NCOMMS-25-27107-T by Liu and colleagues.
Manuscript title: Going wild in banana breeding: the cross-compatibility and multi-omics of Musa cheesmanii
The manuscript presents a detailed investigation into the crossbreeding potential of Musa cheesmanii, highlighting its resistance to Fusarium wilt TR4 and its value as a male parent in banana improvement. The study also contributes a high-quality telomere-to-telomere genome assembly and complementary multi-omics data, providing useful insights into genome evolution and pigmentation traits in Musa species. The findings will be of interest to those working in banana breeding and genomics. However, the manuscript, in its current form, does not align with the broad conceptual scope and interdisciplinary impact required by Nature Communications. We recommend considering resubmission to a more specialised journal focused on crop improvement, plant genomics, or biotechnology, where the work will be more appropriately positioned.
Please see our comments below for further improvement.
Thank you.
General comments
This study contributes meaningfully to banana breeding research by integrating crossbreeding experiments, high-quality genomic data, and multi-omics analyses. The successful hybridisation of Musa cheesmanii with ABB cultivars highlights its potential to enhance disease resistance and yield. Notably, the authors report the first telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly for this species, which adds a valuable resource to the Musa genomics community.
The comparative genomic analysis provides useful insights into chromosomal rearrangements and structural variation among Musa species. Additionally, the integration of transcriptomic and metabolite profiling to investigate pseudostem pigmentation adds depth to the study. The anthocyanin pathway analysis offers a novel angle, although its biological significance remains unclear and may require further refinement.
The rationale for investigating pseudostem colouration is not convincingly presented, and the relevance of this trait to banana breeding is not well established. A more compelling case could have been made by prioritising traits directly linked to agronomic performance, such as disease resistance. For example, a comparative evolutionary analysis of resistance (R) gene families between M. cheesmanii and other Musa species with available high-quality genomes would have added greater value and relevance.
Overall, the manuscript is well-structured, with a logical flow from the problem statement to actionable conclusions, supported by data across multiple levels of analysis.
The use of the first person “we” should be avoided.
Abstract
The abstract provides a clear overview of the study’s objectives and highlights key outcomes, including Fusarium wilt resistance and the generation of productive hybrids. However, the manuscript lacks quantitative data to support several claims in the abstract, particularly those related to hybrid traits such as extended shelf life. Including specific metrics would enhance the credibility of these statements. Furthermore, phrases such as “breakthrough in genetic diversity” are overstated and not fully justified by the results presented. The expression “fully completed genome” is redundant; more precise terminology such as “gap-free” or “telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly” is recommended.
Introduction
The introduction provides a relevant overview of banana breeding challenges and the limited genetic diversity in modern cultivars. The inclusion of Fusarium wilt is appropriate, although it should be explicitly stated that Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense tropical race 4 (TR4) is currently the most devastating fungal disease affecting global banana production. The challenges associated with the activation of endogenous Banana streak virus (eBSV) sequences in hybrids are briefly mentioned, but their impact is understated. In practice, the risk of eBSV activation severely limits the use of B-genome cultivars in breeding programs, and this critical constraint deserves greater emphasis.
These issues help frame the rationale for exploring wild relatives like Musa cheesmanii as alternative genetic resources. However, the specific knowledge gap addressed by this study is not clearly defined. It remains unclear whether M. cheesmanii has never been previously used in breeding programs, or whether this work represents the first comprehensive analysis of its cross-compatibility and genomic potential.
The claim that this study presents “the first fully completed genome in banana” is unsubstantiated and should be revised. Similar high-contiguity, telomere-to-telomere assemblies have already been published for other Musa species, and this work should be positioned in relation to that context.
Finally, the rationale for focusing exclusively on anthocyanins as the drivers of stem pigmentation is weak. Other phenolic compounds, particularly those that contribute to dark or black coloration through oxidative polymerisation (e.g. catechols, L-DOPA, caffeic acid), should also be considered. A more balanced introduction would acknowledge these alternative pathways and set the stage for a broader investigation of pigmentation mechanisms.
Results
This section presents a substantial amount of data, but its impact is limited by gaps in quantitative reporting, inconsistent methodology, and several unsupported claims. While genome assembly and comparative genomics are handled well, data presentation regarding hybrid performance, pigmentation, and qPCR validation require some revision.
Phenotypic evaluation and hybrid performance
• Table 2 lacks critical information. It does not include plant height data, sample sizes, replication numbers, or any measures of variability such as standard deviations. Additionally, the parental line data are absent, making it difficult to contextualise and interpret the performance of the hybrids.
• The number of plants evaluated for each hybrid and parental line should be explicitly reported in both the table and the main text.
• Terms such as “normal seedling percentage” and “seed generation percentage” (lines 173-175) are vague and require clearer definitions to ensure the data are interpretable to readers unfamiliar with the breeding system described.
• The shelf-life claim on line 197, which states an “extended shelf life of 6-9 days,” is not supported by quantitative data. This claim should be backed with comparative measurements between hybrids and parent lines. Similarly, the reference to “excellent taste” is subjective and should be removed unless supported by a sensory evaluation using an established methodology.
Disease resistance data
• While Table 1 presents disease resistance data clearly for the parental lines, no equivalent data are provided for the hybrids. This omission limits the strength of the claim that resistance traits have been successfully transferred.
• A new table should be added to report disease resistance data for the hybrids using the same scoring or index system used in Table 1.
• The “Disease Index” formula referenced in Table 1 should be added to the “Methods” section at least, to ensure transparency and reproducibility.
• The use of “NS” to denote “no symptoms” is inconsistent across the table as NS also appear in the IP column.
Metabolite analysis and pigmentation
• The authors report the detection of numerous low-abundance anthocyanins (Figure S18). However, the authors have not provided any detail in their methods to evaluate the reliability of their compound identification or quantification. Critical information missing includes sample preparation protocols, chromatographic separation parameters, MS/MS acquisition settings, and criteria used for compound identification. This lack of transparency is particularly concerning given that several anthocyanins share identical m/z values, making chromatographic resolution and MS/MS spectral interpretation essential for accurate compound differentiation. For metabolite quantification the authors should report whether they used any standards for quantification. Without this information, it is difficult to assess whether the low-abundance signals are from true analytes or are analytical artifacts.
• Following this, the authors suggest that the black stem colouration is due to accumulation of specific anthocyanins presented in Supplementary figure 18b. Whilst the authors have reported statistical significance in compound accumulation, given their extremely low abundance (for example 0.02 ug/g pelargonidin-3-O-arabinoside) compared to other identified compounds (eg. in S18a procyanidin B2 is reported at around 300 ug/g for both M. cheesmanii and the green stemmed Musa acuminata) is this difference likely to be biologically relevant in creating the black stem phenotype? The authors should note that dark brown or black colouration can come from sources other than anthocyanins. Oxidation of phenolics which have two neighbouring hydroxyl groups can lead to the formation of quinone-like structure which can further undergo polymerisation making brown/black colouration. Examples include caffeic acid, catechol, catechin, dopamine and L-DOPA. Dopamine and L-DOPA have previously been detected in various banana tissues at high concentrations. Additionally, as the first 3 compounds share many of the genes/enzymes with the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway, the authors should consider adjusting the manuscript (including transcriptome analysis) to encompass all phenolics rather than only anthocyanins.
Transcriptomic validation (qPCR)
• The claim that transcriptomic findings were validated by qPCR (lines 377-378) is misleading. For example, the gene F3’H is not statistically significant based on Supplementary Figure 15a, and there is no presented qPCR data for PAL2 or BGLU26, even though these genes are mentioned.
• The qPCR methodology is also not described. The manuscript should include details about cDNA synthesis protocols, primer sequences, and amplification conditions in the “Methods” section.
• To support transparency and reproducibility, the authors should also consider providing raw Ct values as a supplementary table.
• Supplementary Figure 8a appears to be nearly identical to Figure 4a in the main text. To avoid redundancy, one of these figures should be removed.
Minor revisions and editorial suggestions
• The authors should ensure consistent terminology and formatting across all tables and figures, particularly for labels and abbreviations.
• All abbreviations should be defined upon first use in each table or figure, even if they are explained elsewhere in the manuscript. For example, “eBSV” should be redefined as “endogenous banana streak virus” where it first appears.
Discussion
This is a good discussion supported by a solid foundation of relevant literature.
Certain sections, such as the paragraph beginning at line 509, primarily summarise results rather than examining their broader implications within the context of existing research.
The discussion does not consider some of the practical challenges associated with the use of M. cheesmanii in breeding programs. These may include low hybrid recovery rates, the potential for linkage drag, and the complexity of backcrossing strategies. Additionally, phrases such as “revolutionary breakthrough” and “remarkable productivity” are used in the text without sufficient supporting evidence and do not align with the otherwise analytical tone.
Expanding the discussion to include resistance genes, specifically identifying the types of loci involved, could add value. Comparing these loci to those found in other published Musa genomes, and considering their potential implications for breeding strategies, would provide additional depth and relevance.
The structure of the discussion may be improved by the inclusion of subheadings to support clarity and assist reader navigation. Several paragraphs are lengthy and would benefit from being divided into smaller units. Although the intended audience is likely to have technical expertise, certain terms could be clarified to increase accessibility. For example, “eBSV” could be restated as “endogenous banana streak virus,” and terms such as “segregation distortion” and “structural heterozygosity” could be accompanied by short explanations.
The presentation of data may be strengthened through brief agronomic interpretation. For instance, a girth to height ratio of 0.225 could be described as exceeding the threshold associated with resistance to lodging.
Finally, the discussion could also benefit from consideration of future directions, such as whether similar traits may be found in other underutilised Musa species or what risks could emerge from the widespread deployment of M. cheesmanii in breeding programs.
Methods
Critical methodological details are missing in several areas, which limits the reproducibility and rigour of the study.
The description of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense TR4 inoculation lacks essential information. The origin of the fungal strain, its vegetative compatibility group (VCG), and the inoculation protocol (particularly the spore concentration and method of application) are not provided. In addition, the criteria used to evaluate external and internal symptoms of infection, and how disease severity was scored or calculated, are not adequately described.
Hybrid evaluation is similarly underdeveloped. Terms such as “seed set,” “seed generation,” and “normal seedling” (lines 592-593) are ambiguous and require precise definitions. The section describing hybrid assessment (lines 592-597) lists variables that were evaluated but does not explain how these measurements were conducted. Sample sizes for hybrid offspring are also not reported, and replication details are entirely missing.
The anthocyanin analysis lacks transparency, with key methodological details missing. Specific recommendations for improving this section are outlined in the Results critique above.
qPCR validation of transcriptomic data is not described at all. There is no information about cDNA synthesis, primer sequences, qPCR reaction conditions, or normalisation strategies. To improve transparency and reproducibility, the authors should include these details in the methods and provide raw Ct values in a supplementary table.
Finally, a specific section on statistical analysis should be included.
Tables and figures
• The overall quality and readability of the tables and figures is good. However, Figures 1 and 2 would benefit significantly from higher-resolution images and improved formatting to enhance visual clarity.
• In Figure 2, scale bars are missing from all panels and should be added to ensure interpretability, particularly for morphological comparisons.
• In Table 2, the definition of “plant stature” is placed in the footnotes, should also be added to the main text (Methods). Table 2 needs to include data from parental lines, plant height measurements, standard deviations, and the number of replicates. A new table reporting hybrid disease resistance should be created, modelled on Table 1.
• Figure 4, panel (e), which presents RGA2 polymorphisms, requires clearer labelling to highlight the nonsense mutation (T→A at 3,687 bp).
• Figure 4 and Supplementary Figure 8 present nearly identical phylogenetic trees. To avoid redundancy, one of these should be removed.
• Figure legends throughout should be made more descriptive, especially when referring to multi-panel figures.
End of report

Reviewer #2:
I read the manuscript titled "Going wild in banana breeding: the cross-compatibility
and multi-omics of Musa cheesmanii" with great interest. I should underline that my
expertise is mainly in genome assembly rather than banana genomics. I would like to
congratulate the authors on this genome assembly. Even though it is of low
complexity, they generated a substantial amount of diverse sequencing data and
produced a high-quality reference genome for Musa cheesmanii. Here are my main
concerns about this study.
We sincerely thank you for your thoughtful evaluation of our manuscript and are
encouraged that you consider our reference genome to be of high quality despite the
relatively low complexity of this species. We also thank you for raising important
concerns, which we have carefully considered and addressed in the revised
manuscript as detailed in our point-by-point responses below.
Sequencing Data and Assembly Methods:
The authors generated interesting sequencing data and combined two long-read
technologies with Hi-C data, which is better than the current standard. However, they
used methods that are generally not employed for reference genomes: NextPolish and
TGS-GapCloser. Most genomes from projects like VGP, dToL, ATLASea, or BGE
are based on purge_dup (instead of Purge_Haplotigs), YaHS (instead of 3D-DNA),
and are manually curated using Pretext (instead of Juicebox). This is not a problem at
all, but the authors should provide adequate validation of their assembly at different
stages.
I would expect a supplementary table containing standard analyses such as BUSCO,
Merqury, and KAT for the assembly obtained at each step: raw assembly, polished
assembly, purged assembly, gap-closed assembly, and final assembly. This would
allow monitoring the impact of each tool on the assembly.
Thank you for this valuable suggestion. As recommended, we have performed
assembly evaluations at different stages of the pipeline, including the primary HiFi
assembly, polished primary assembly, purged assembly, Hi-C anchored assembly,
gap-closed assembly, and the final assembly. For each stage, we assessed the quality
using BUSCO, Merqury, and KAT in order to monitor the impact of each tool on
assembly quality. The results show consistently high performance across all stages.
Detailed results are now provided in Supplementary Table 6 and Supplementary Fig.
3.
Use of TGS-GapCloser:
The authors used TGS-GapCloser, which is rarely used in the generation of reference
genomes. I understand the temptation to get an assembly without gaps, but I would be
very cautious about the accuracy of these gap-closed regions. The authors should
clearly indicate their position in the genome and provide at least local validation using
long-read coverage and Hi-C map visualization.
Thank you for this important comment. We agree that careful validation of gap-closed
regions is essential. In response, we have clearly marked the positions of all four
previously gapped regions in the figures used for visual validation. We examined the
breakpoint regions using long-read coverage and confirmed that the sequences used to
close the gaps span the breakpoints. We also added Hi-C heatmaps to support the
assembly. However, we would like to note that gap4 is located in a highly repetitive
rDNA array region on chromosome 10. This type of complex region is commonly
associated with assembly breaks and is known to display strong internal Hi-C
interactions but weak connections to neighboring regions, making it difficult for Hi-C
data alone to resolve. Similar patterns have been observed in other Musa genome
assemblies, including those of M. acuminata, M. balbisiana, and cultivated Cavendish
banana. Fortunately, our ONT long reads enabled us to confidently fill this region.
Relevant supporting figures have been added (see Supplementary Figures 23-24).
Chromosomal Inversion:
I was curious to know if the inversion detected in chromosome 5 with Macuminata
and Mschizocarpa occurs at the same position in Musa cheesmanii. Can the authors
provide more information and details about this inversion? Validation of breakpoints
would be of interest.
The inversion on chromosome 5 observed in M. acuminata and M. schizocarpa is not
present in M. cheesmanii, as shown in Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 9. In addition,
we have validated the detected structural variation breakpoints using long-read
alignments (Supplementary Fig. 10), which confirm the presence of these structural
variations, including this inversion.
Data Availability:
The assembly and gene annotation were not available from the NGDC database nor
from the Banana Genome Hub. Please provide access to the genome.
The assembly and gene annotation are available on Figshare:
http://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.25658835
Specifically, the genome assembly file is Mch.reverse.w0.renumbering.fasta, and the
genome annotation file is Mch.reverse.renumbering.gff.

Reviewer #3:
Review of Manuscript ID NCOMMS-25-27107-T by Liu and colleagues.
Manuscript title: Going wild in banana breeding: the cross-compatibility and
multi-omics of Musa cheesmanii
The manuscript presents a detailed investigation into the crossbreeding potential of
Musa cheesmanii, highlighting its resistance to Fusarium wilt TR4 and its value as a
male parent in banana improvement. The study also contributes a high-quality
telomere-to-telomere genome assembly and complementary multi-omics data,
providing useful insights into genome evolution and pigmentation traits in Musa
species. The findings will be of interest to those working in banana breeding and
genomics. However, the manuscript, in its current form, does not align with the broad
conceptual scope and interdisciplinary impact required by Nature Communications.
We recommend considering resubmission to a more specialised journal focused on
crop improvement, plant genomics, or biotechnology, where the work will be more
appropriately positioned.
Please see our comments below for further improvement.
Thank you.
We sincerely thank you for the thorough and constructive comments, which have
been extremely valuable in improving our manuscript. Bananas are among the most
important staple crops worldwide, yet they face the severe threat of Fusarium wilt.
Cultivated bananas already possess a narrow genetic base, and the predominant
reliance on M. acuminata subspecies as breeding parents has further intensified this
limitation, leaving the crop even more vulnerable to diseases. Identifying new
parental resources is therefore of critical importance. However, progress has been
extremely limited for decades due to the crop's triploid nature (resulting in low
fertility) and its lengthy breeding cycles. Through extensive resistance evaluations
and crossbreeding efforts, we have identified M. cheesmanii as a promising candidate
parent. Together with complementary multi-omics analyses, our work not only
addresses urgent challenges in banana improvement but also provides essential
background knowledge of this species. We have carefully revised the manuscript
according to your suggestions, and we hope that this version now meets the high
standards and interdisciplinary impact expected for publication in Nature
Communications.
General comments
This study contributes meaningfully to banana breeding research by integrating
crossbreeding experiments, high-quality genomic data, and multi-omics analyses. The
successful hybridisation of Musa cheesmanii with ABB cultivars highlights its
potential to enhance disease resistance and yield. Notably, the authors report the first
telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly for this species, which adds a valuable
resource to the Musa genomics community.
The comparative genomic analysis provides useful insights into chromosomal
rearrangements and structural variation among Musa species. Additionally, the
integration of transcriptomic and metabolite profiling to investigate pseudostem
pigmentation adds depth to the study. The anthocyanin pathway analysis offers a
novel angle, although its biological significance remains unclear and may require
further refinement.
The rationale for investigating pseudostem colouration is not convincingly presented,
and the relevance of this trait to banana breeding is not well established. A more
compelling case could have been made by prioritising traits directly linked to
agronomic performance, such as disease resistance. For example, a comparative
evolutionary analysis of resistance (R) gene families between M. cheesmanii and
other Musa species with available high-quality genomes would have added greater
value and relevance.
We agree with this comment and complemented the study a comparative evolutionary
analysis of resistance (R) gene families between M. cheesmanii and other Musa
species (see lines 339-361 and Figure 4).
Overall, the manuscript is well-structured, with a logical flow from the problem
statement to actionable conclusions, supported by data across multiple levels of
analysis.
The use of the first person “we” should be avoided.
We have carefully reviewed the use of the first person “we” throughout the
manuscript and revised it where possible.
Abstract
The abstract provides a clear overview of the study’s objectives and highlights key
outcomes, including Fusarium wilt resistance and the generation of productive
hybrids. However, the manuscript lacks quantitative data to support several claims in
the abstract, particularly those related to hybrid traits such as extended shelf life.
Including specific metrics would enhance the credibility of these statements.
Furthermore, phrases such as “breakthrough in genetic diversity” are overstated and
not fully justified by the results presented. The expression “fully completed genome”
is redundant; more precise terminology such as “gap-free” or “telomere-to-telomere
(T2T) genome assembly” is recommended.
We appreciate these helpful comments. We have incorporated quantitative data to
substantiate the claims about the enhanced hybrid traits, revised overstated
expressions to ensure a more objective presentation, and replaced “fully completed
genome” with “telomere-to-telomere, gap-free genome assembly”.
Introduction
The introduction provides a relevant overview of banana breeding challenges and the
limited genetic diversity in modern cultivars. The inclusion of Fusarium wilt is
appropriate, although it should be explicitly stated that Fusarium oxysporum f. sp.
cubense tropical race 4 (TR4) is currently the most devastating fungal disease
affecting global banana production. The challenges associated with the activation of
endogenous Banana streak virus (eBSV) sequences in hybrids are briefly mentioned,
but their impact is understated. In practice, the risk of eBSV activation severely limits
the use of B-genome cultivars in breeding programs, and this critical constraint
deserves greater emphasis.
Thank you for your helpful comments. In response, we have made two key revisions
in the Introduction to better highlight the issues you raised. First, to emphasize the
threat posed by Fusarium wilt, we added the sentence: “However, global production is
increasingly threatened by Fusarium wilt, a fungal disease caused by Fusarium
oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc), with tropical race 4 (Foc_TR4) currently recognized
as the most devastating fungal pathogen affecting banana cultivation worldwide”
(lines 54-57). Second, regarding the activation of eBSV, we revised the text to: “The
use of M. balbisiana is severely constrained by the risk of activating endogenous
banana streak virus (eBSV), especially under stress or during in vitro culture, which
can lead to spontaneous viral expression in hybrids and compromise plant health and
yield. This genetic instability not only limits the use of B-genome cultivars in banana
improvement programs but also hampers global germplasm exchanges due to the risk
of eBSV activation into an infectious episomal form” (lines 97-102). We believe these
updates better reflect the severity and practical implications of these challenges in
banana breeding.
These issues help frame the rationale for exploring wild relatives like Musa
cheesmanii as alternative genetic resources. However, the specific knowledge gap
addressed by this study is not clearly defined. It remains unclear whether M.
cheesmanii has never been previously used in breeding programs, or whether this
work represents the first comprehensive analysis of its cross-compatibility and
genomic potential.
Thank you for highlighting this important point. As far as we are aware, there are no
published studies reporting the use of M. cheesmanii in banana breeding programs,
nor comprehensive evaluations of its cross-compatibility or genomic potential. We
also selected the Silk and Plantain cultivars to assess the potential genetic contribution
of M. cheesmanii to these hybrids, as these two AAB cultivars are currently the only
ones with high-quality reference genomes that contain B-genome components. As
shown in Supplementary Fig. 5, M. cheesmanii contributes very little, if at all, to these
two common hybrids. This suggests that M. cheesmanii has not yet been used in
breeding programs for these cultivars, highlighting its undervalued potential for future
breeding. To clarify the novelty and relevance of our work, we have revised the
manuscript accordingly to emphasize this knowledge gap: “However, M. cheesmanii
has not previously been utilized or systematically examined in banana breeding
research, and its cross-compatibility and genetic characteristics remain unexplored,
indicating the need for in-depth characterization to support its use in breeding” (lines
125-129).
The claim that this study presents “the first fully completed genome in banana” is
unsubstantiated and should be revised. Similar high-contiguity, telomere-to-telomere
assemblies have already been published for other Musa species, and this work should
be positioned in relation to that context.
Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that our original wording was too strong.
Although our Musa cheesmanii assembly is more complete than previously published
Musa genomes (being gap-free and including all telomeric sequences), we have
revised the sentence in the manuscript to describe this more accurately. The updated
sentence now reads: "A telomere-to-telomere (T2T) gap-free genome assembly of M.
cheesmanii is also presented, representing the most complete banana genome to date,
with all telomeres identified and no assembly gaps" (lines 137-139).
Finally, the rationale for focusing exclusively on anthocyanins as the drivers of stem
pigmentation is weak. Other phenolic compounds, particularly those that contribute to
dark or black coloration through oxidative polymerisation (e.g. catechols, L-DOPA,
caffeic acid), should also be considered. A more balanced introduction would
acknowledge these alternative pathways and set the stage for a broader investigation
of pigmentation mechanisms.
We appreciate your valuable comment. We have revised the Introduction to
acknowledge that, in addition to anthocyanins, the oxidative polymerization of
phenolic compounds (e.g., catechols, L-DOPA, caffeic acid) may also contribute to
the dark pigmentation observed in banana pseudo-stems (lines 116-118).
Results
This section presents a substantial amount of data, but its impact is limited by gaps in
quantitative reporting, inconsistent methodology, and several unsupported claims.
While genome assembly and comparative genomics are handled well, data
presentation regarding hybrid performance, pigmentation, and qPCR validation
require some revision.
Phenotypic evaluation and hybrid performance
• Table 2 lacks critical information. It does not include plant height data, sample sizes,
replication numbers, or any measures of variability such as standard deviations.
Additionally, the parental line data are absent, making it difficult to contextualise and
interpret the performance of the hybrids.
We appreciate your constuctive comment. Table 2 has been revised to include a
complete set of data for both parental lines and hybrids. Plant height (here evaluate
using pseudostem height) and other key agronomic traits, including bunch weight, and
plant stature, are now reported with mean values and standard deviations (mean ± SD).
Detail information on sample sizes, replication numbers, and experimental design is
provided in both Table 2 and the Methods section (Please see lines 691-700).
• The number of plants evaluated for each hybrid and parental line should be
explicitly reported in both the table and the main text.
The number of plants evaluated for each trait has now been reported in both the
Tables and the Methods section. For the resistance evaluation in Table 1, each
accession was represented by 15 plants. Due to asynchronous development among
different accessions, the sample sizes are not identical across all traits in Table 2. For
the reproductive performance traits (seed set, seed germination and normal seedling),
we evaluated more than 3,000 fruits, 300 seeds, and 80 hybrid progenies, replicated
three times. Pseudostem colour was assessed in over 100 plants. For the agronomic
traits (bunch weight, pseudostem height, and plant stature), each parental line was
represented by 10 randomly selected plants from population. For the F1 hybrid
combinations, considering differences in cross-compatibility as well as the stability
and agronomic performance of F1 progeny phenotypes, we selected the 10 hybrid
lines that exhibited the best fruit quality with each line represented by 5 plants.
Details are shown in Table 1 & 2, and lines 651-652, 696-700.
• Terms such as “normal seedling percentage” and “seed generation percentage”
(lines 173-175) are vague and require clearer definitions to ensure the data are
interpretable to readers unfamiliar with the breeding system described.
Thank you for this comment. The term “normal seedling” has now been clarified as
“seedlings with healthy and regular appearance” (line 204). "Seed set" refers to the
average number of seeds produced per fruit (line 202). In addition, “seed generation
percentage” has been corrected to “seed germination percentage” (line 202).
• The shelf-life claim on line 197, which states an “extended shelf life of 6-9 days,” is
not supported by quantitative data. This claim should be backed with comparative
measurements between hybrids and parent lines. Similarly, the reference to “excellent
taste” is subjective and should be removed unless supported by a sensory evaluation
using an established methodology.
We have added quantitative data on shelf-life determination, showing that the edible
period of the hybrid 'Haijiao No. 1' (M. cheesmanii × 'Yulin') is longer than that of its
maternal parent 'Yulin' (Supplementary Fig. 1). In addition, a sensory evaluation was
conducted, indicating that 'Haijiao No. 1' had a more favorable taste compared with
'Yulin' (Supplementary Table 1). Nevertheless, to ensure objectivity, the term
“excellent taste” has been replaced with “favorable taste” in the revised manuscript.
Disease resistance data
• While Table 1 presents disease resistance data clearly for the parental lines, no
equivalent data are provided for the hybrids. This omission limits the strength of the
claim that resistance traits have been successfully transferred.
Thank you for pointing out this important issue. We have now included the disease
resistance data for the hybrids and their maternal parents. These results have been
integrated into Table 1.
• A new table should be added to report disease resistance data for the hybrids using
the same scoring or index system used in Table 1.
The hybrids were evaluated using the same scoring system as the parental lines,
ensuring methodological consistency. To facilitate comparison and maintain a concise
presentation, the results were added to Table 1 rather than placed in a new table.
• The “Disease Index” formula referenced in Table 1 should be added to the “Methods”
section at least, to ensure transparency and reproducibility.
The formula for calculating the “Disease Index” has been added to the Methods
section. Please see lines 663-665.
• The use of “NS” to denote “no symptoms” is inconsistent across the table as NS also
appear in the IP column.
For table 1, the “NS” in the IP column has been changed to “NA” for clarity. The
table note now reads: “NA: Not Applicable, as incubation period cannot be calculated
due to absence of symptoms.”
Metabolite analysis and pigmentation
• The authors report the detection of numerous low-abundance anthocyanins (Figure
S18). However, the authors have not provided any detail in their methods to evaluate
the reliability of their compound identification or quantification. Critical information
missing includes sample preparation protocols, chromatographic separation parameters,
MS/MS acquisition settings, and criteria used for compound identification. This lack of
transparency is particularly concerning given that several anthocyanins share identical
m/z values, making chromatographic resolution and MS/MS spectral interpretation
essential for accurate compound differentiation. For metabolite quantification the authors
should report whether they used any standards for quantification. Without this
information, it is difficult to assess whether the low-abundance signals are from true
analytes or are analytical artifacts.
Thank you for pointing out this important issue. We have revised the Methods section
to include additional details on metabolite identification and quantification (lines
921-936).
• Following this, the authors suggest that the black stem colouration is due to
accumulation of specific anthocyanins presented in Supplementary figure 18b. Whilst
the authors have reported statistical significance in compound accumulation, given
their extremely low abundance (for example 0.02 ug/g pelargonidin-3-O-arabinoside)
compared to other identified compounds (eg. in S18a procyanidin B2 is reported at
around 300 ug/g for both M. cheesmanii and the green stemmed Musa acuminata) is
this difference likely to be biologically relevant in creating the black stem phenotype?
The authors should note that dark brown or black colouration can come from sources
other than anthocyanins. Oxidation of phenolics which have two neighbouring
hydroxyl groups can lead to the formation of quinone-like structure which can further
undergo polymerisation making brown/black colouration. Examples include caffeic
acid, catechol, catechin, dopamine and L-DOPA. Dopamine and L-DOPA have
previously been detected in various banana tissues at high concentrations.
Additionally, as the first 3 compounds share many of the genes/enzymes with the
anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway, the authors should consider adjusting the
manuscript (including transcriptome analysis) to encompass all phenolics rather than
only anthocyanins.
We appreciate your insightful comment and fully agree that pigmentation is not solely
determined by anthocyanins. In response, we have expanded our analysis to include
genes involved in the oxidative metabolism of phenolic compounds, which are known
to contribute to dark or black pigmentation through enzymatic polymerization.
Specifically, we examined the expression of polyphenol oxidase (PPO), peroxidase
(POD), and DOPA decarboxylase (DDC), key enzymes involved in these pathways
(lines 418-420). However, our results showed no significant upregulation of these
genes in the black-pseudostem samples, suggesting that phenolic compounds may
contribute less to pseudostem pigmentation than anthocyanins. In addition,
considering that metabolites with low abundance are less likely to contribute
significantly to the black pseudostem coloration, we only selected the top 10 most
abundant metabolites in the black pseudo-stem (Mchb) of M. cheesmanii for
comparison. Based on this analysis, we found that the delphinidin-based pathway may
play an important role in the black coloration of M. cheesmanii pseudostems, and we
have revised the corresponding results accordingly (lines 451-463).
Transcriptomic validation (qPCR)
• The claim that transcriptomic findings were validated by qPCR (lines 377-378) is
misleading. For example, the gene F3’H is not statistically significant based on
Supplementary Figure 15a, and there is no presented qPCR data for PAL2 or
BGLU26, even though these genes are mentioned.
Thank you for pointing out this important issue. We have revised the description of
the qPCR validation to ensure it accurately reflects the results. Specifically, we
clarified that BGLU26 and PAL2 failed to amplify, and F3'H showed higher
expression in black pseudo-stems but not significantly. The revised text now provides
a more precise and detailed account of the differential expression analysis. Please
refer to lines 432-439.
• The qPCR methodology is also not described. The manuscript should include details
about cDNA synthesis protocols, primer sequences, and amplification conditions in
the “Methods” section.
Thank you for this pointing this out. We have now added the relevant details on cDNA
synthesis protocols, primer sequences, and amplification conditions in the Methods
section (lines 909-920).
• To support transparency and reproducibility, the authors should also consider
providing raw Ct values as a supplementary table.
We thank you for this suggestion. We have now provided the raw Ct values in Source
Data (sheet 5) to support transparency and reproducibility.
• Supplementary Figure 8a appears to be nearly identical to Figure 4a in the main text.
To avoid redundancy, one of these figures should be removed.
We agree with your suggestion and have removed Supplementary Figure 8a to avoid
redundancy with previous Figure 4a (now Figure 5a) in the main text.
Minor revisions and editorial suggestions
• The authors should ensure consistent terminology and formatting across all tables
and figures, particularly for labels and abbreviations.
We have carefully checked all tables and figures to ensure consistency in terminology,
labels, and abbreviations throughout the manuscript.
• All abbreviations should be defined upon first use in each table or figure, even if
they are explained elsewhere in the manuscript. For example, “eBSV” should be
redefined as “endogenous banana streak virus” where it first appears.
All abbreviations have been checked and are now defined upon their first appearance
in each table and figure.

### Reviewer 1

Many thanks for the opportunity to review this revised manuscript.
The authors have addressed all my previous concerns and I think the manuscript makes an extremely valuable contribution to the future of banana breeding, as well as providing an abundance of multi-omic data that other researchers can draw upon.

### Reviewer 2

The authors addressed all my requests and comments. I just have one last point regarding the assembly quality. The authors ran BUSCO, KAT, and Merqury after each step of the assembly process, and, as observed in many other projects, polishing tends to lower the quality of the assembly (as shown by the Merqury results and also by the loss of one complete BUSCO gene). I think the authors should indicate in the manuscript (for example lines 746 and 760) that polishing appears to have reduced the quality of some loci in the assembly.

### Reviewer 3

Review of Manuscript ID NCOMMS-25-27107A by Dr Huang and colleagues.
Manuscript title: Going wild in banana breeding: the cross-compatibility and multi-omics of Musa cheesmanii
General comments
The authors have made a commendable effort and have substantially improved the manuscript, addressing many of the reviewers’ previous concerns. However, a few issues remain that should be revised before the manuscript can be considered for publication.
Minor revisions:
1. The newly included Supplementary Figure 1 illustrates the improved shelf life of Yulin compared to its offspring; however, the data presented are limited to peel discolouration. In the figure legend, the authors note that “Yulin begins to collapse externally, with the pulp turning sour and rotting. In contrast, Haijiao retains its robust shape and desirable flavour.” Similar to comments made on the original manuscript, these observations lack supporting quantitative data. The authors are encouraged to include simple, quantifiable indicators of shelf-life to strengthen their claims. Parameters such as titratable acidity, pulp firmness, total soluble solids, weight loss, or respiration rate are routinely used to assess postharvest quality and could be readily incorporated. These measurable attributes would provide a more objective basis for evaluating fruit longevity and quality over time.
2. In addition, statements referring to “desirable flavour” should be supported by appropriate evidence, such as sensory evaluation or compositional profiling (for example, measurements of sugars, acids, or volatile compounds). Including these analyses would substantiate the claim and enhance the credibility of the reported quality improvements.
3. The comparison of flavonoid metabolite profiles is presented in Supplementary Figure 22 and Figure 6c; however, M. acuminata data are not shown in the bar charts of Figure 6c. The authors state that M. acuminata was excluded because it belongs to “clade A and is more distantly related to M. cheesmanii”. This rationale seems insufficient. Furthermore, in their analysis, the authors state that 4 anthocyanins, rutinoside and glucoside derivatives of delphinidin and petunidin, account for the black phenotype of M cheesmanii based on higher accumulation in the black stem compared to green stem. However, M. acuminata, which lacks black stem colouration, clearly accumulates higher levels of these compounds as shown in Supplementary Figure 22. This suggests that these anthocyanins alone do not account for the black phenotype, which may instead be derived from polymeric or derivatives of these compounds. However, they state they “compare with authentic standards” (line 934) and quantify “using external standards” (line 935). The authors should explicitly list which authentic standards were used for compound quantification. Given that they use MRM data for quantitation and that ionisation efficiency (and hence detection) can vary greatly between compounds, accuracy of the reported concentrations depends on the availability of appropriate authentic standards. If standards for all compounds were not available, the authors should clarify this and present the results as relative comparisons rather than as absolute quantifications (Fig 6c).

Example: line 412 “…replicates (Supplementary Fig. 17)” should be (Supplementary Fig. 17a) same for line 422 should be (Supplementary Fig. 17b)
